as in the other great reforms he meant to introduce for the good and benefit of all Jewry, which would surely have been
worthy to bring the redemption near, had the generation merited to see his plan carried out and to live by his godly
ways. But sins caused his sun to set before its time: he lived there only about a quarter of a year. Suddenly the
destroyer came. On the New Moon of Iyar 5478 [1718] the lamp of Israel of the holy community of Lwów went out; their
light was darkened, their joy turned to mourning, and all the land of Poland wept and mourned at the evil news. They
mourned and lamented him as the one unique in his generation; even the lords of the provinces of Poland lamented him.

It is impossible to set down in a book the good name that my father left among Israel and among the neighbours ⟨S: "the
uncircumcised"⟩; it would not be believed if it were told. For our many sins, it was heard that the lords said: "The
Messiah of the Jews came to Poland, and they killed him." So I heard when I passed there half a year later, travelling to
visit my father's grave ⟨S: a word, not read⟩; and all along the long road I heard people telling wonders of him ⟨S: a
four-line note, partly read: "… and he did good things in Lwów …"⟩. Most of them I have forgotten because of all that
befell me afterwards.

When the news of his death reached Germany, they lamented him in all the communities with great bitterness, and said:
"Woe to the generation that has lost its leader and captain!" The Sephardi community in London also did him great honour
at his death [a] ⟨S: a three-line note, partly read: "as is done for kings …"⟩. And a trustworthy man who was in
Amsterdam told me that at the time they eulogised my father there, Ḥakham A. [b] cried out with a full mouth: "Truly
I have sinned against Ḥakham Tzvi, of blessed memory!" Several of the famous rabbis ⟨S: a long note, partly read; its
place is not certain: "[the synagogue] hung with black, and all … the parnassim and the elders sat on the ground …
mourning, lamenting and eulogising him like the mourning for the destruction of Jerusalem"⟩ in the land of Poland —
namely the geonim R. Joshua, who is now head of the court of the holy community of F[rankfurt], and R. … [c] ⟨S:
"Eleazar"⟩, who was afterwards head of the court in the holy community of Amsterdam, and R. Meir, head of the court of
Tykocin — tore their garments for him and sat on the ground, keeping mourning for one day. And my ears heard one of the
great men of the generation say of my father that the world was not worthy to use so holy a vessel, in whom was the soul
of one of the early Tannaim.

For our many sins his days were evil, as we have seen from a little of much of his affairs, and from the hard events and
fearful times that passed over him. He was persecuted and insulted many times by the thorns of our people "at the edge of
the camp", because of his uprightness, righteousness and integrity, for he showed no favour in Torah. For this godly
trait the presumptuous and the moneyed men multiplied against him; they "embittered him, and shot at him, and hated him,
the archers" (Gen. 49:23); "those given to change"

ומשנים, נזדווגו אל עין משפט, עין שעשתה מדה"ד בעולם בקשו לסמותה, אבל אין אחד שהתגרה בו מלחמה שלא נכוה בגחלתו, סוף שלקה בגופו וממונו, דקב"ה תבע ביקריה, ויארכו הדברים לספר, כל מה שקרה לכמה שהיו במעלה עליונה רמה מאד, שפגעה בהם קללתו, לסוף ירדו מנכסיהם לדיוטא תחתונה, וכמה נעקרו ר"ל הם וביתם. רק שנים שלשה גרגרים אספר לדור אחרון, למען ידעו ויבינו וישכילו זאת, וראו כמה נאמנים דברי חז"ל הזהר בגחלתן וכו', וכל מקום שנתנו בו חכמים עיניהם וכו', כאשר ראינו כ"פ בעינינו, וישימו על לב, כי אש שורפת היא מנפש עד בשר, ליגע במשיחי ה' עבדיו הנאמנים, שומרי בריתו עושי מלאכתו באמונה, לחזק בדקי הדת להעמידה על תלה ועוסקים בתורה לשמה .
והאחד שקבל ענשו בפומבי, מה שלא נשמע דוגמתו, מפורסם מאד בעולם, הוא ארון גאקיש, פרנס כמה שנים בק"ק אשכנזים דאמשטרדם, והיה עשיר מכמה פעמים מאה אלפים זהובים, תקיף ועצום שבכל הקהל שנזכר בעו"ה ממנו ומחביריו השנים יודא פורינץ ומרדכי כהן. אלה היו ג' פושעי ישראל, שהוסרו ממינוי פרנסות ע"י שהחזיקו במחלוקת של החזנים כנז"ל, ועד"ז היו לו לאויבים גם לאמ"ה ז"ל, מחמת שלא היה מסייעם לדבר עבירה, לעקר ולשרש את הכת החלושה כחפצם לראות בם כמש"ל באורך, מאז נהפכו לו לאויבים, ועשו לאמ"ה ז"ל כל הבזיונות והקלונות שיכלו לעשות, להכאות לב צדיק, וגאקיש יותר מכולם כלפי חוצפתו הגדולה העצומה בטבעו; והיו מלעיגים עליו, גם מצד עשרו הרב, אם אמנם היה ג"כ עשוי שלא ביושר, על כן אבד העושר ההוא בענין רע, כאשר בא כן הלך. הוא גדל כלב וקרא שמו... בקיצור עמדו על חייו של אמ"ה ז"ל. ולשנים האחרים, חבריו הנ"ל, לא ארך הזמן, כי מיד אחר נסע איש האלהים משם ירדו מנכסיהם נקיים ומתו בענין רע: יהודה פרינץ נחנק. עוד פרנס אחר שראינו, שאיני רוצה להזכיר שמו [א], שהיה ג"כ מכת שונאיו, נפל מעגלה של פאשט ונשברה מפרקתו. אך לגאקיש האריך הי"ת: כמה שנים אחר זאת נשאר בגדולה, וחזר לפרנסתו ומעלה כבתחלה, ואסף עשרו של קרח והתנהג בחוצפה גדולה ועזות, והיה העולם מתמיהים, מאחר שראו בחוש שכל שונאי אמ"ה ז"ל נפלו ונשברו נוקשו ונלכדו בשחיתותם, כסבורים המקום וותרן הוא לו, כי המתין לו

joined together against the eye of judgement — the eye that executed the attribute of justice in the world, they sought
to blind it. But there was not one who waged war against him who was not burned by his coals: in the end he was struck in
body and in money, for the Holy One, blessed be He, demands His honour. It would take long to tell all that befell several
who stood at a very high and lofty level, whom his curse reached: in the end they came down from their wealth to the
lowest level, and several were uprooted, God save us, they and their households. I will tell only two or three grains
of it for the last generation, so that they may know, understand and consider this, and see how true are the words of the
Sages, "beware of their coals" (Avot 2:10) and "wherever the Sages set their eyes" and so on, as we have seen many times
with our own eyes; and let them take to heart that it is a fire that burns "both soul and body" (Isa. 10:18) to touch the
Lord's anointed, His faithful servants, who keep His covenant and do His work in faith, who repair the breaches of the
religion and set it on its foundation, and engage in Torah for its own sake.

The first, who received his punishment in public, the like of which has not been heard, and who is very well known in
the world, is Aaron Gokkes, parnas for several years in the Ashkenazi community of Amsterdam. He was rich many times a
hundred thousand gulden, the strongest and mightiest in the whole community, mentioned (for our many sins) together with
his two companions, Yuda Prinz and Mordecai Kohen. These were the three sinners of Israel who were removed from the office
of parnas for keeping up the controversy of the cantors, as mentioned above. For that reason they were enemies of my
father too, because he would not help them in a sinful thing — to uproot and root out the weak faction as they wished —
as I have written above at length. From then on they turned into his enemies, and did my father every insult and
disgrace they could, to wound the heart of the righteous; and Gokkes more than them all, because of his great and
enormous insolence by nature. They mocked him, also on the strength of their great wealth — though it too had been made
dishonestly; therefore that wealth "perished in an evil venture" (Eccl. 5:13): as it came, so it went. He raised a dog
and called its name … In short, they rose up against my father's life.

As for his two companions mentioned above, it was not long: immediately after the man of God left there, they lost their
possessions and died an evil death. Judah Prinz was strangled. Another parnas whom we saw, whose name I do not wish to
mention [a], who was also of the faction of his enemies, fell from a post wagon and broke his neck. But with Gokkes the
Blessed One was long-suffering: for several years after this he remained in greatness, went back to his office and his
standing as before, gathered the wealth of Korah and behaved with great insolence and brazenness. The world wondered,
since they had seen with their own eyes that all my father's enemies had fallen and been broken, snared and caught in
their own pits; they thought that the Omnipresent was being indulgent with him, for He waited for him

יותר מעשרים שנה אחריהם; אך פתאום לפתע בא שברו עת פקודתו, ועל דבר קטן של הבל נתפס מן השופט דאמשטרדאם; בתחלה היה יכול לפצותו בדבר מועט, גם אחר כך היה יכול לפדות עצמו באיזה מאות זהובים, אך הוא העשיר יענה עזות, ושוב רצה לתת עשרת אלפים זהובים שישלחהו חפשי מבית האסורים, וכבר היה נאות לו השופט שנתן עיניו בממון הרב, אך מן השמים היה שבא במצודה רעה, שלא יכול לצאת ממנה ונפל תורא כו', כי השררה גזרה לעכבו בבית הסוהר, ברזל בא נפשו וישם בסד רגלו, ונדון במשפט מות כגנב מוחלט, והוציאוהו ביום שבת קודש לדונו ולהמיתו כמות נבל, ושברו המקל עליו, וקראו לפניו גזר דינו במקום המשפט אצל התלייה לעיני רבבות ב"א. אח"ז עשו לו חסד להניחו בחיים גרועים ממות, והפשיטוהו ערום והלקוהו בשבטים, עשו בו שפטים, והשאירו לו נפשו לשלל, וחזרו והוליכוהו לתפיסה, וגזרו עליו לענותו בעבודה קשה של הנסירה בעצי בראזיל [א] הקשים כמו אבן, שהמגרה משקלה כמה מאות ליטרין; בה מענישים לחייבי מיתה שהשיגו חסד. ככה נגזר עליו שיעמוד בבית הכלא ההוא כל ימי חייו ויעשה המלאכה הנ"ל דבר יום ביומו כאשר קצבו לו, וכבר היה זקן יותר מבן שבעים שנה. שם בבית הסוהר חתם חייו אחר שנתיים ימים, וממונו אבד, אע"פ שלא שלחה השררה ידי' בממונו, הלך הכל לטמיון, ומבניו כמה שיצאו לתרבות רעה ומתחלה כשבאה עליו הצרה לא חשבה, כי היה דבר קל בראשיתו כנ"ל, אך הוא היה כמצחק בעיניו; אח"כ כשראה הענין ברע מתגבר, עלה קצת ברעיוניו ממה שעשה לאמ"ה ז"ל, ודאג מעט ושלח לק"ק לבוב דבר מועט, לאסוף מנין עשרה מישראל שיבקשו בעדו מחילה על קברו של הצדיק אמ"ה ז"ל, אבל נטל אפופסין שלו משלם כמש"ל, ונעשה למשל ולשנינה בכל העולם, כי היה מפורסם מאד בכל המדינות, בין השכנים כמו בין הישראלים בהפלגת העושר . ונדפסו מן המאורע הלז כמה חבורים וספרים בלעז, ובתוכם נזכר ג"כ מה שעשה לאמ"ה ז"ל בכל שאר מעשיו בביאור, והיה קדוש השם גדול בעולם, שהכל ראו והודו, כי בסבת מה שעשה לצדיק באה עליו הצרה הזאת, מידו היתה לו זאת, ראו רבים וייראו ואמרו: כמה גדולים דברי חכמים ונאמנים, כי גדולים צדיקים במיתתן, וכל שנעשה רושם הזה באיש רשום הזה, מה שלא נודע כיוצא בו.

more than twenty years after them. But suddenly his ruin came, the time of his reckoning. Over a small, empty matter
he was arrested by the magistrate of Amsterdam. At first he could have settled it for a small sum; even afterwards he
could have bought himself free for some hundreds of gulden; but "the rich man answers roughly" (Prov. 18:23). Later he
wanted to give ten thousand gulden to be released from prison, and the magistrate, who had set his eyes on the large
sum, was already willing; but it was from heaven that he had come into an evil net from which he could not get out —
"and the ox fell", and so on. For the authorities decreed that he be kept in prison; "the iron entered into his soul"
and his feet were put in the stocks (Ps. 105:18); he was condemned to death as an outright thief. They brought him out on
the holy Sabbath to judge him and put him to death like a villain; they broke the staff over him and read out his
sentence before him at the place of judgement by the gallows, in the sight of tens of thousands of people.

After this they did him the "kindness" of leaving him a life worse than death. They stripped him naked and flogged him
with rods — they executed judgements on him — and left him his life as a spoil. They took him back to prison and
sentenced him to the hard labour of sawing Brazil wood [a], which is as hard as stone, with a saw that weighs
several hundred pounds: with it they punish those condemned to death who have been shown mercy. So it was decreed that he
stay in that prison all the days of his life and do this work day by day, as was set for him; and he was already an old
man of more than seventy. There in the prison he ended his life after two years. His money was lost: though the
authorities did not lay a hand on his money, it all went to waste; and several of his sons went to evil ways.

At first, when the trouble came on him, he thought little of it, for it was a light thing at the beginning, as said; it
was like a joke in his eyes. Afterwards, when he saw the matter growing worse, what he had done to my father rose a
little in his thoughts, and he worried a little, and sent a small sum to Lwów to gather a quorum of ten Jews to ask
forgiveness for him at the grave of the righteous man, my father. But he received his due in full, as I wrote, and became
a byword and a taunt in all the world; for he was very famous in all the countries, among the neighbours ⟨S: a word,
perhaps "the uncircumcised"⟩ as among the Jews, for his extreme wealth. Several works and books were printed about this
affair in the vernacular ⟨S: perhaps "in the language of the gentiles"⟩, and in them is also told plainly what he did to
my father, together with all his other deeds. It was a great sanctification of the Name in the world, for everyone saw
and admitted that this trouble came on him because of what he had done to the righteous man: "this was from his hand".
Many saw it and feared, and said: "How great and true are the words of the Sages — the righteous are greater in their
death." That such a mark should be made on so marked a man — the like of it was not known.

הן אלה קצות דרכי האדם הגדול אמ"ה ז"ל, אשר לא הניח כמותו בתורה, ביראה ובמדות, ביחוד בשנאת בצע ואהבת צדק אין על עפר משלו; ובהוראה היה יחיד בזמנו, וכל חכמי דורו באשכנז ופולין שאבו ממקורו מים חיים, אחרי דברו לא שנו, כאשר ישאל איש בדבר האלקים, כי היו פתוחים בזכרונו כל שערי אורה, במקרא במשנה בגמרא, בטורים בפוסקים ראשונים ואחרונים, וש"ת קדמונים חדשים עם ישנים, ושאר ידיעות, ובקי בכמה לשונות, הכל כמונח בקופסיה, וצח לשון, בעל זכרון עצום מאד, ולב חריף ושכל ישר מתון ומסיק, ועל כולם חסידותו, קדושתו וזהירתו בכל דקדוקי מצות בדיוק גדול, ומחזר אחר קיומן בכל לב ובכל נפש, וכל מגמתו לזכות הרבים, והיה שוקד על הלמוד יום ולילה לא ישבות, לא מצאו אדם אלא עוסק בתורה, שינתו כשלש או ארבעה שעות לכ"ה בכ"ד שעות, ואכילתו ושתיתו כאכילת ושתית תינוק קטן, ועם זה זוהר תמונתו כאיש אלקים, יפה

And as his curse did not return empty, but tore the strong-armed "with the crown of the head" (Deut. 33:20) — the sons
of tumult it punished and killed — so his blessing was whole and did not go out empty, but brought great abundance of
good and plenty: "the blessing of the Lord, it makes rich" (Prov. 10:22). I will set out only two faithful witnesses as
examples.

The first is my kinsman R. A. N., who at the time my father left Amsterdam was his attendant. He did not depart from his
tent, and served the rabbi without expecting a reward, though he was roaming after his own living to seek his bread; he
had no benefit from my father's money. He also had to support his old and poor father and mother and bring them their
food. Even so he did not leave my father, and stood before him at all times to serve him, doing his needs and the needs
of his house day by day, more than any day-labourer. When my father set out on his journey towards Poland, this man, who
had feared God from his youth, wanted to leave his father and mother and come with my father to serve him on the way,
following him to a land he did not know, so as not to leave the righteous man without service. But my father ⟨S: a
four-line note, partly read⟩ would not let him travel with him and turned him from his purpose; so he stayed in
Amsterdam, as I will tell further, with God's help.

The second is the leader R. Aberle London, who was blessed by him when he parted from Hamburg, where my father had sat
some days over his lawsuits with his brother-in-law E. P., as said. R. Aberle had been left empty of all his wealth,
stripped of his possessions because of the hard judgement and the hard opponent mentioned above; and my father, in his
blessing, assured him not to worry, for he was sure that his fortune would rise and quickly flourish for good. And so it
was, for no word left his mouth in vain: not many days passed before R. Aberle earned several times a hundred thousand
Reichstaler. R. Aberle himself recognised that the righteous man's blessing had stood by him; so when he heard of my
father's death he vowed a hundred ducats to his orphans — but his vow was not kept, as I will write, with God's help.

These are the edges of the ways of that great man, my father, who left none like him in Torah, in fear of Heaven and in
character — above all in hating gain and loving justice there was none on earth like him. In practical ruling he was
unique in his time; all the sages of his generation in Germany and Poland drew living water from his spring, and "after
his words they spoke not again", as a man inquires of the word of God. For all the gates of light stood open in his
memory: Bible, Mishnah and Gemara, the Ṭurim, the codifiers early and late, responsa old and new ⟨S: a five-line note,
partly read: "… books of …, grammar and philosophy …"⟩, and other knowledge. He was expert in several languages, all as
if lying ready in a box; eloquent; of very great memory, a sharp heart and an upright mind, deliberate and conclusive.
And above all, his piety, his holiness and his care over every detail of the commandments, with great precision, pursuing
their fulfilment with all his heart and all his soul; all his aim was to bring merit to the many. He was diligent in study
day and night without rest; no one ever found him other than engaged in Torah. His sleep was about three or four hours at
most in twenty-four, and his eating and drinking like the eating and drinking of a small child. With this, the radiance of
his appearance was like that of a man of God: handsome


צורה תואר ומראה מהודרים, פרצופו נוטה לעיגול ומראהו לבן אדמדם, מצחו גדול, חוטמו מעט ארוך בנרתיק [א] התחתיתו (?) ופה קטן נאה מאד ועצום תמיד, שפתותיו שושנים, לסתות פנויות משערות כאילו היה מגולח, וזקנו עשוי מקיף מאוזן לאוזן, כעטרה מתחת לחייו כערוגות הבושם, ושבולת הזקן ארוך דק מחודד מחולק לשנים, מעברתו רחבה בדיקניה, שערותיו כגוון הזהב ומסולסלים, בשרו רך וענוג ולא נראה לו שער על חזהו, תוארו בכלל כמלאך האלקים נורא, ומאוים בהבטת עיניו [ב], ומקבל את כל אדם בסבר פ"י, דבורו צח שפתו ברור מללו, ומכיר בכמה לשונות כנ"ל, וכן לשון כתיבותיו בלה"ק תמהר לדבר צחות ברור וקצר, נוח לכל אדם רחמן ואב לאביונים, וקשה כברזל כנגד קשה עורף, ולשבר גיד ברזל בעל זרוע, מפניהם לא ייחת לאשר חמוץ, ולשבר מתלעות עול ישליך מפיהם טרף, חסיד ועניו לירא ה', ומכניע גאון זדים וגאים, ועם המדברים גבוהה ידבר קשות, לא נשא פנים בתורה, ומורא ב"ו לא עלה על ראשו מימיו, ילאה. הקולמוס לבאר כל מעשיו הנוראים, ומדותיו האלקיות ודבקותו בה', לעבוד עבודתו לשמור משמרתו בכל לב ובכל נפש מאד, וכבר רשמתי ממנו קצת בילדותי, ובאו בדפוס בקונטרס "יציב פתגם" דרוש הספדו, ולא הגעתי לחצי כבוד.
גם זכהו הי"ת להביא לדפוס בחייו ח"א מס' תשובותיו, בדפוס נאה ומשובח ונייר טוב, עודנו על כסא הרבנות דאמשטרדם. והספר יקר חשוב מאד בעיני המשכילים, כאחד מספרי תשובות הקדמונים, ונמכר ביוקר, והניח גם קבוצת כת"י מחידושי תורה ושו"ת ובגפ"ת ודרוש, אך שלטו בהן ידי זרים. זמן רב היו מונחים בליסא, אחר הביאתם זוגתי ז"ל, ולא נגעתי בהם והיו מונחים אצלה זה שבע ועשרים שנה כאבן דאין לה הופכים עד סוף שנת תקי"ז; בא הנה, ר"ה שנתקבל לאב"ד בלונדון, והפציר בי לתתם אליו ע"מ שיוציאם לאור הדפוס ובהיותו נקרא על שמו, ומסרתי בידו.

in form, in features and in looks, splendid. His face tended to roundness, his complexion white and ruddy; his forehead
large; his nose a little long, "in its sheath" [a] below (?); his mouth small and very handsome, always closed; his
lips lilies; his cheeks free of hair, as if shaved. His beard ran around from ear to ear, like a crown under his jaws,
"like beds of spices" (Song 5:13); the point of the beard long, thin and sharp, divided in two, broad in its fullness. His
hair was the colour of gold and curled; his flesh soft and tender, and no hair was to be seen on his chest. His appearance
as a whole was like an angel of God, awesome, and fearsome in the gaze of his eyes [b]. He received every man with a
pleasant face. His speech was eloquent, "his lips speak clearly" (Job 33:3) ⟨S: a seven-line note, partly read⟩. He knew
several languages, as said; and the language of his writings in the holy tongue likewise "is ready to speak plainly"
(Isa. 32:4), clear and brief.

He was gentle to every man, merciful and a father to the poor, and hard as iron against the stiff-necked, to break the
iron sinew of the strong-armed; he was not dismayed before them, "to relieve the oppressed" (Isa. 1:17), to break the jaws
of the unrighteous and make him drop the prey from his teeth. He was pious and humble towards those who feared the Lord,
and humbled the pride of the presumptuous and the arrogant; with those who speak haughtily he spoke harshly. He showed no
favour in Torah, and the fear of flesh and blood never came upon his head. The pen would weary of telling all his awesome
deeds, his godly qualities and his cleaving to the Lord — to serve Him and keep His charge with all the heart, all the
soul and all the might. I already set down a little of it in my youth, and it came out in print in the pamphlet Yatziv
Pitgam, the sermon of his eulogy; and I did not reach half of his honour.

The Blessed One also granted him to bring to print in his lifetime the first part of his responsa, in a fine and
excellent printing on good paper, while he was still on the rabbinical seat of Amsterdam. The book is precious and very
highly regarded by the learned, as one of the books of the early responsa, and it sells dearly. He also left a collection
of manuscripts of Torah novellae, responsa, notes on Gemara, Rashi and Tosafot, and homilies; but strangers' hands took
control of them. For a long time they lay in Lissa. Afterwards my wife, of blessed memory, brought them, and I did not
touch them; they lay with her these twenty-seven years, "like a stone that no one turns over", until the end of the year
5517 [1757]. Then R. H. came here ⟨S: a word, not read⟩, who had been received as head of the court in London, and pressed
me to give them to him, on condition that he bring them out to the light of print, and since he bore his name; and I
handed them over to him.

As I wrote, he sometimes had controversies for the sake of Heaven with the Ashkenazi sages of his generation, as can be
seen in his responsa, § 2 — above all, that he wrote bitterly against R. Abraham Broda, who was then head of the yeshivah

קפדנות ביניהם, אספרה הלום מעשה שהיה, ספור ששמעתי מפה קדוש אמ"ה ז"ל: הרב הנ"ל השתדך עם בנו לבת ישראל פערשט, והיה בהמבורג על נישואי בנו, אז יש]ב[ אמ"ז הרב מהר"ז מירלש על כסא הרבנות דג"ק, הוא עשה סעודה על הרב מוהר"א ז"ל ובנו ומחו', ואמ"ה ז"ל היה אז בשנת אבלו על אביו ז"ל, על כן לא הלך לסעודה הנ"ל, אך בתוך הסעודה הנ"ל הלך אמ"ה ז"ל לבית חמיו בלי קריאה, ולהקביל פני הת"ח האורח ולשאול לו שלום, ולקח עמו תלמידיו הלומדים מופלגים שבקלויז דאלטונא, ונתנו לו שלום למוהר"א, וישאלהו לאמ"ה ז"ל עד האידנא מ"ט לא שאל לי מר לשלמא, להקדים לבוא אליו להקביל פניו בבית מחותנא. מיד כשמוע אמ"ה ז"ל כי בקש גדולה לעצמו בפה מלא. לנגד כל העומדים עליו נתפעל מזה, וענה בחכמה: אנא מתניתא וגמרא ידענא, ההוא עובדא דפ"ק דחגיגה דרבי ור"ח דאזלי באורחא, אמרי אי איכא צורבא מרבנן הכא ניזיל ונקבל אפיה, א"ל איכא חד ומאור עינים הוא אזלו לגביה וכו' [א], ש"מ שדין האורח שילך לקבל פני הת"ח שבעיר תחלה. ויוסף ויאמר אליו: הנה על כרחך תודה שאינך גדול בדורנו מרבינו הקדוש בדורו, גם ודאי שאני עכ"פ איני פחות הערך בדור הזה מההוא צ"מ בדור ההוא, בהכרח כי אותו ת"ח לא ידע ממנו רבי כלל, ולא שמע שמו מעולם, כי על כן שאל איכא צ"מ הכא, מכלל שנעלמה מציאותו לגמרי מרבי, ומר ידע ממני עכ"פ שאני מצוי פה, א"כ הדין היה נותן שיבוא אלי ויקבל פני תחלה לפחות, שהרי רבי שאל איכא צ"מ הכא, ניזיל ונקבל אפיה, אע"פ שהיה רבי נשיא של כל ישראל, רצה לילך להקביל פני ת"ח שבעיר, יהא מי שיהא, לכן שאל מר שלא כהוגן, ואני לפנים משורת הדין עשיתי, שבאתי הלום הפעם הזאת; ולהתנצל על שלא באתי לסעודה שנקראתי אליה, שת"ח מסב בה, כי אסור לי לבוא על סעודה של רשות מחמת אבלי, ואעפ"כ לכבודו באתי עתה. אז כשמוע מוהר"א ז"ל שקפחו אמ"ה ז"ל בתשובתו הנצחת, הוסיף עוד לדבר אליו: א"כ היה לו למר לשלוח תלמידיו אלי לקבל פני ולדרוש שלומי, וכך עשיתי אני לגדול אחד שבא למקומי, ולא הלכתי בעצמי אליו, אלא אך שלחתי את תלמידי במקומי לד"ש. ויענהו אמ"ה ז"ל אני אין לי תלמידים. ויוסף עוד מוהר"א לדבר אליו ויאמר, ומי הם אלה שבאו עם מעכ"ת, השיב אמ"ה ז"ל, אלה הם חברי, ובזה
[א] חגיגה (דף ה').

strictness between them. I will tell here something that happened, a story I heard from the holy mouth of my father.
The said rabbi made a match for his son with the daughter of Israel Fürst, and he was in Hamburg for his son's wedding.
My grandfather, the rabbi R. Zalman Mirels, then sat on the rabbinical throne of the Three Communities; he made a feast
in honour of the rabbi R. Abraham, his son and his relative by marriage. My father was then in his year of mourning for
his own father, so he did not go to the feast. But during the feast my father went, uninvited, to his father-in-law's
house, to greet the visiting scholar and ask after his welfare; and he took with him his students, the outstanding
scholars of the Kloyz of Altona. They greeted R. Abraham, and he asked my father: "Why has the master not greeted me
until now, coming first to visit me at the house of his relative?"

As soon as my father heard that he sought greatness for himself so openly, before all who stood there, he was stirred by
it, and answered wisely: "I know Mishnah and Gemara. There is the story in the first chapter of Ḥagigah, of Rabbi and
R. Ḥiyya who were walking on the road. They said: 'If there is a young scholar here, let us go and greet him.' They were
told: 'There is one, and he is blind' — and they went to him, and so on [a]. From this we learn that the law is that
the guest goes first to greet the scholar of the town." And he went on: "You must admit that you are not greater in our
generation than our holy Rabbi was in his; and surely I am at least of no lesser standing in this generation than that
young scholar in that one. Rabbi, of necessity, did not know of that scholar at all and had never heard his name — that
is why he asked 'Is there a young scholar here?' — so his existence was quite unknown to Rabbi; whereas you, sir, at
least knew that I am here. So the law would have it that you come to me and greet me first, at the least. For Rabbi asked
'Is there a young scholar here? Let us go and greet him', and though Rabbi was the prince of all Israel, he wished to go
and greet the scholar of the town, whoever he might be. So you asked improperly; and I acted beyond the letter of the law
in coming here this time. As for my not coming to the feast to which I was invited, at which a scholar is reclining: it
is forbidden to me to attend an optional feast because of my mourning. Even so, for your honour I have come now."

When R. Abraham heard that my father had bested him with his triumphant answer, he spoke to him again: "If so, the master
should have sent his students to me to greet me and ask after my welfare. That is what I did for a great man who came to
my town: I did not go to him myself, but sent my students in my place to ask after his welfare." My father answered him:
"I have no students." R. Abraham spoke again and said: "Then who are these who came with your honour?" My father answered:
"These are my colleagues." And with this

השתיקו מענין זה. אז פתח אמ"ה ז"ל בשמעתא דאתמול, כי ביום ש"ק דרש הרב מוהר"א ז"ל בבה"כ דאלטונא, והיה שם אמ"ה ז"ל ג"כ, ושמע ושתק, כי היסב פניו אל הכותל, ולא רצה להכניס עמו בפלפול וויכוח בבה"כ. כך היה דרכו ז"ל ומנהגו עם הדורשים, שלא להשגיח בהם אם טוב אם רע יאמרו; רק הפעם מצא מקום להקפיד, כל קבל די רוח יתירא חזא בדעתיה דמוהר"א, לכן א"ל אמ"ה: אתמול בדרשה שלו תירץ קושיא (ולא ידעתי מה היתה) והוא טעות ושיבוש, ונכנסו בפלפול, עד שנתייגע הרב מוהר"א, וקרא לבנו החתן: משה תענה אותו! ואמ"ה ז"ל לא הי"ל בן בעת ההיא, ובתו הילדה היתה אז שם בבית א"ז. אז קרא אמ"ה: מרים בתי בואי ותעני אליו! ונפרדו בכעס. אבל מ"מ היה אהבה בסוף, כי כעת מחר שלח מוהר"א ז"ל למדן אחד אל אמ"ה ז"ל לבקש ממנו מחילה בעדו, והודיעו שקבל עליו להתענות יום אחד על שהקניטו. מכאן נראה שהיה ג"כ חסיד מוהר"א ז"ל, אף ע"פ שלא היתה רוחו שפלה, ומאז נתפייסו ועבדו רבנן שלמא. מ"מ כשבאה תשובת מוהר"א ז"ל לאמ"ה ז"ל, אמר נפל מיד להראות שלא הי"ל להתגאות עליו כל כך
ואגב אספר ג"כ מה שאירע עוד: שדרש הרב ר"א חתנו של מרדכי כהן, וגער הרב מוהר"ג בהרב ר"א, שלפ"ד דרש איזה דבר של דופי. ור"א לעג עליו וא"ל: אם היה באמת הדבר שדברתי ושאמרתי שלא כהוגן, לא היה שותק לי חכם צבי, אמ"ה ז"ל שידוע שהוא ]איננו[ נושא פנים בתורה, והוא היה באותו מעמד ושתק. וכשהגידו הדברים לאמ"ה אמר: מעתה לא טוב הדבר שאני עושה, כי בני אדם נכשלים בשתיקתו וחושבים כהודאה, ומאז והלאה לא הלך עוד לבה"כ בשעת דרשה.

they let that subject drop. Then my father began on the previous day's discourse. On the holy Sabbath R. Abraham had
preached in the synagogue of Altona, and my father was there too; he listened and kept silent, for he turned his face to
the wall and would not enter into debate and argument with him in the synagogue. That was his way and his custom with
preachers: not to pay attention to them, whether they said good or bad. Only this time he found reason to take offence,
"because an excessive spirit" (Dan. 6:4) he saw in R. Abraham's mind. So my father said to him: "Yesterday, in your
sermon, you answered a difficulty" (I do not know what it was) "and it is a mistake and an error." They entered into
debate, until R. Abraham grew weary and called to his son the bridegroom: "Moses, answer him!" My father had no son at
that time, and his little daughter was there in my grandfather's house. So my father called: "Miriam, my daughter, come
and answer him!" And they parted in anger.

But in the end there was love after all: the next day R. Abraham sent a scholar to my father to ask forgiveness on his
behalf, and let him know that he had taken upon himself to fast one day for having provoked him. From this we see that
R. Abraham too was a pious man, though his spirit was not lowly; and from then on they were reconciled, and "the rabbis
made peace". Even so, when R. Abraham's responsum reached my father, he said: "He fell at once" — to show that he should
not have been so haughty towards him.

By the way I will also tell what happened another time. The rabbi R. A., son-in-law of ⟨S: "and there was also the rabbi
R. …, head of the court of N.S., who married his son to the daughter of"⟩ Mordecai Kohen, preached, and the rabbi R. M. G.
rebuked R. A., because in his opinion he had preached something blameworthy. R. A. mocked him and said: "If what I said
and expounded were really improper, Ḥakham Tzvi would not have let it pass in silence" — my father, who was known [not]
to show favour in Torah — "and he was present on that occasion and kept silent." When they told my father these words, he
said: "From now on what I am doing is not good, for people stumble through my silence and take it for agreement." From
then on he no longer went to the synagogue at the time of a sermon.


עד הנה הגיע ספורי זה על אודותיו של אמ"ה ז"ל, מה שנשארו בזכרוני עוללות, כי הרבה שמעתי ושכחתי, ויתר מזה מה שלא ידעתי כל עיקר, כי בן שבע עשרה שנה הייתי בהפרדי מאתו ז"ל, וברוב מילי דאבא קטן הוינא. כ"ש שלא יכולתי לדעת פרטי מאורעותיו, שהרבה קדמוני בטרם הייתי, שכבר היה קרוב לארבעים בלדת אותי, ועד שהגעתי לכלל בר מצוה כבר היה יותר מבן חמשים, וכל שמושי אותו היה בארבע וחמש שנים, בצער גדול בצרי המחלוקת, ומהם עבר זמן רב בגלות טלטול קשה, ומחליים רעים ונאמנים, וכמה תמורות ופגעים, ומה שידעתי מפי השמועה רובו שכחתי בסיבת המון שינוי העתים המבעתים שעברו עלי, אשר אם זכרתי ונבהלתי, עד שמחמת הסבות הרבות והרעות מסופקני אם אוכל לספרם, כחול ירבון אם אזכרם, ואם באתי לכתוב כולן אין מספיקים, קולמוסין ויריעות ודיוטות אם יהיו מי אפיקים; לכן אספרם דרך קצרה, מטפס ועולה.
קודם שאתחיל בספור קורותי, אודיע נאמנה שלא באתי לכלל זה, למען ספר שמי ותהלתי, כי יודע אני בעצמי, שאין בי שום מעשה לא תורה לא חכמה, לא גדולה היתה לי לנחלה, שאתפאר ואתגדר בה, הלואי שלא אעלה על גליוני, מה שיגלה חסרוני, אך יודע כל שער עמי שבחרתי בשפלות, מיום עמדי על דעתי היותי מכיר ערכי ומומי, על כן מזה הטעם עצמו לא אכפת לי ולא אחוש, נודע לכל שפלותי, כי רק האמת אהבתי. ומחמת שלש טעמים באתי לידי מדה זו, לבאר בכתב קורותי, ולא אמנע מלהודיע לי"ח [א] כל עניני כפי אשר תשיג יד האפשרות, ואם לא אגיע לכולו, לפחות אזכור כל הנזכר אצלי בעת, ואשר עבר עלי עד הנה; ואמנם הסבה החזקה שהניעה אותי לזה היא להודיע חסד ה' עלי מנעורי, אף אם רבות צררוני, לא יאומן כי יסופר אמר על בן בגבורים דאפשר לאדם לסבול אחת מני אלף, האם כח אבנים כחי אם בשרי נחוש, וכל שכן שהייתי רך לאבי ולאמי ענוג וחלוש, וכמעט הייתי בכל רע, ומקרה קשה ופגע, בלי הפסק רגע, ומכולם הצילני הי"ת ב"ה, ועזרני עד כה,
[א] ר"ת: ליוצא חלצי.

So far my account of my father has come: what remained in my memory, gleanings only. For much I heard and forgot, and
beyond that there is what I never knew at all; I was seventeen years old when I parted from him, and in most of my
father's affairs I was a child. All the more I could not know the details of his life, much of which came before I
existed: he was nearly forty when I was born, and by the time I reached the age of bar mitzvah he was already over fifty.
All my service of him was in four or five years, in great distress, in the troubles of the controversy; and much of that
time passed in exile, in hard wandering, and in evil and lasting illnesses, and in many changes and mishaps. What I knew
by hearsay I have mostly forgotten, because of the many changes of the fearful times that passed over me; "when I remember,
I am dismayed" (Job 21:6). Because of the many and evil events ⟨S: a seven-line note, partly read: "… the ever-renewed …
which never let me go … many events"⟩ I doubt whether I can tell them; "they are more in number than the sand" (Ps. 139:18)
if I recall them; and if I set out to write them all, pens, sheets and ink would not suffice, were they streams of water.
So I will tell them briefly, climbing step by step.

Chapter 2 begins herein the manuscript and in Bick's edition

Before I begin the story of my own life, I declare faithfully that I did not come to this in order to make my name and my
praise known. I know of myself that I have no deed, no Torah, no wisdom, and no greatness as an inheritance, in which to
glory and pride myself; would that I do not set down on my pages what reveals my faults. But "all the gate of my people
knows" (Ruth 3:11) that I chose lowliness from the day I came to understanding, knowing my worth and my blemish. For this
very reason I do not care or mind that my lowliness becomes known to all, for I love only the truth. For three reasons I
came to this practice of setting down my experiences in writing, and I will not hold back from making known to my
descendants [a] all my affairs, as far as possible; and if I do not reach all of it, at least I will mention all that
I remember at this time, and what has passed over me until now.

The strongest reason that moved me to it is to make known the Lord's kindness to me from my youth. Though "many a time
have they afflicted me" (Ps. 129:1), it would not be believed if told; I would say even of a mighty man that a man can bear
only one in a thousand of them — "Is my strength the strength of stones? Is my flesh of brass?" (Job 6:12) — all the more
since I was tender and delicate in my father's and my mother's eyes, and weak. I was in almost every evil, every hard event
and mishap, without a moment's pause; and from all of them the Blessed One saved me and helped me until now,

יסור יסרני ולמות לא נתנני, לא נטשני לכלות ח"ו, כאב את בן ירצני ויקם על סלע רגלי, אם אמרתי מטה רגלי, ימין ה' רוממה תסעדני ותתמכני, לכן אמרתי אספרה שמך ה' לאחי ולזרעי וי"ח, ולמען לא אשבח חסדיו, ולא תשכחי נפשי כל גמוליו, ובתוך רבים אהללנו, כי יעמוד לימין אביון, להושיע משופטי נפשי, רובי נפלאותיו אשר עשה עמדי הדל באלפי, אודיע לדור אחרון, לכן שמעו כל יראי אלהים, אשר עשה לנפשי תמיד בכפי, שפתי רננות יהלל פי, ובקולמוסי רוב חסדו אביע, הודיות בקול אשמיע, למען ידעו דור אחרון, בנים יולדו יקומו ויספרו לבניהם, ויודו לה' כי טוב כל"ח, כי הושיע נפש אביון מיד בנים מרעים; וזאת שנית: לחזק ידים רפות דכאי רוח ונכאי לבב, והנעלבים והנרדפים על לא חמס בכפם, כמוני היום על צוארי נרדפתי משונאי חנם ומשלמי רעה ]תחת[ טובה, ישטנוני תחת רדפי טוב, יראו רבים וייראו ויבטחו בה', ישימו באלהים כסלם, ולא ישכחו מעללי אל, לא יפול לבבם מהמון עריצים ומשטמת בעלי חצים; ושלישית, למען יזרח שמש צדקתי, ולא תשכון עליו עננה, מפני רשעים זו שדוני, אויבי בנפש יקיפו עלי, והוציאו עלי דבה להבאישני ביושבי הארץ, להשמידני חרף בידם בשקריהם ופחזותם, שנתפשטו בכל עבר ופנה בכל הארץ בשתם, ובודאי ישארו הרבה כתבי פלסתר שלהם בעולם זמן מה, לכן ההכרח אלצני לברר עסקי נגד ה' ואדם, ויצא כאור צדקי ימלט אי נקי, והאמת עד לעצמי, והנה הוא לי כסות עינים ולבני וי"ח הש"י.
ואחל בספור קורותי, למען דעת צדקות ה' אשר לא יבושו קויו, ולא יכלמו לנצח כל החוסים בו, עזרה בצרות נמצא מאד, כאשר ראיתי בעיני פעמים רבות, אם אמרתי בחפזי נגזרתי מארץ חיים נגזרתי, ואומר אך חושך ישופני תהום יסובבני, ולילה אור בעדני, ואם אמרתי מטה רגלי, חסדך ה' יסעדני, גם כי אשב בחושך ה' אור לי ישוב אפו וינחמני, ויתן בפי שיר חדש תהלה לאלהינו, וה' ישים דברו בפי, ויהיה עם שפתי וקולמוסי ויודע תהלתו לדורות הבאים. הנה הודעתי למעלה, כי בעת עבורי חלה אמ"ה חולי השחורה בסבת אבוד ממונו, ויהי חליו כבד מאד, עד שכמעט נתייאשו מרפואתו, לולי רחמי שמים שגבר עליו והחזירהו לאיתנו. איזה ימים לפני עת

"He has chastened me sore, but He has not given me over to death" (Ps. 118:18); He did not forsake me to be
destroyed, God forbid, "as a father the son in whom he delights" (Prov. 3:12); "He set my feet upon a rock"
(Ps. 40:3). "When I said, My foot slips, Your mercy, O Lord, held me up" (Ps. 94:18); "the right hand of the Lord is
exalted" (Ps. 118:16) — it supported and upheld me. So I said: I will declare Your name, O Lord, to my brothers and to
my descendants, so as not to forget His kindnesses — "forget not, my soul, all His benefits" (Ps. 103:2) — and "among
the many I will praise Him, for He stands at the right hand of the needy, to save him from those who judge his soul"
(Ps. 109:30–31). The greatness of the wonders that He did for me, the poorest of my clan (Judg. 6:15), I will make
known to the last generation. "Come and hear, all you who fear God, what He has done for my soul" (Ps. 66:16), "my life
is continually in my hand" (Ps. 119:109); "my mouth shall praise You with joyful lips" (Ps. 63:6), and with my pen I
will pour out His great kindness and make thanksgiving heard aloud, "that the generation to come might know, the
children yet to be born, who shall arise and tell their children" (Ps. 78:6), and give thanks to the Lord, for He is
good, for His kindness endures for ever; "for He has delivered the soul of the needy from the hand of evildoers"
(Jer. 20:13).

And this is the second reason: to strengthen weak hands, the crushed in spirit and the broken in heart, the insulted and
the persecuted who have no violence in their hands — as I am today. "Upon our necks we are persecuted" (Lam. 5:5) by
those who hate me without cause and repay evil for good; "they are my adversaries because I follow the good"
(Ps. 38:21). "Many shall see and fear, and shall trust in the Lord" (Ps. 40:4); "that they might set their hope in God,
and not forget the works of God" (Ps. 78:7); and their hearts shall not fail before the multitude of tyrants and the
hatred of the archers.

And the third: that the sun of my righteousness may shine, and no cloud rest on it, "from the wicked who despoil me, my
deadly enemies who compass me about" (Ps. 17:9), who spread an evil report about me to make me odious to the
inhabitants of the land (Gen. 34:30), to destroy me — a reproach in their hands — with their lies and their recklessness,
which spread in every direction through all the land, to their shame. Surely many of their libels will remain in the
world for some time. So necessity forced me to set out my affairs plainly before God and man, that my righteousness may
go forth as the light (Ps. 37:6); "He will deliver the innocent" (Job 22:30); and the truth is a witness for me. Let it
be to me "a covering of the eyes" (Gen. 20:16), and for my sons and descendants, may the Blessed One keep them.

I begin the story of my life, to make known the righteous acts of the Lord: that "those who wait for Him shall not be
ashamed" (Isa. 49:23), and none who take refuge in Him will be confounded for ever. "A very present help in trouble"
(Ps. 46:2), as I have seen with my own eyes many times. "I said in my haste, I am cut off" (Ps. 31:23) from the land of
the living; and I said, "Surely the darkness shall cover me" (Ps. 139:11), "the deep surrounded me" (Jon. 2:6), "and the
night shall be light about me"; "when I said, My foot slips, Your mercy, O Lord, held me up"; "though I sit in darkness,
the Lord is a light to me" (Mic. 7:8); "His anger is turned away and He comforts me" (Isa. 12:1); "He has put a new song
in my mouth, praise to our God" (Ps. 40:4). May the Lord put His word in my mouth and be with my lips and my pen, and may
His praise be made known to the generations to come.

I have told above that while my mother was carrying me, my father fell ill with melancholy because of the loss of his
money. His illness was very severe, until they almost despaired of his recovery, had not the mercy of Heaven prevailed
over him and restored him to his strength. Some days before the time

of my birth he came home from the bath of Ems, where he had taken the cure of that spring between Passover and Shavuot.
He came to Altona after his wife, my mother the rebbetzin, of blessed memory, had given birth to me, on the fifteenth of
Sivan 5457 [1697] [a]. He circumcised me himself — after the despair, when the commandment had already been given to
another mohel — and brought me into the covenant with a great double joy: that he had returned to his health as before,
and that he had been given a son after despairing of one, for until then he had only daughters; and so he fulfilled the
commandment of circumcision with rejoicing.

I was the fourth child and the first son, tender and an only one to my father and my mother, after my mother had borne
three daughters. My parents trembled and quaked over me greatly, and I was brought up on their knees as a darling child,
in great pleasure, tenderness and longing. With all this my father hurried to put me into school when I turned three, so
that in my fifth year I had already finished learning the tractate Berakhot ⟨S: perhaps "plunder"⟩. I was so diligent at
the book that my companions of my own age ran after me and had not yet learned to read the prayers at that time. But
afterwards he held back from putting my brothers, born after me, into the teacher's house while they were such tender
children, for he said that it had weakened me.

If I set out to tell all that passed over me in the years of my childhood, the story would be very long, besides what is
hidden and forgotten from me. I will mention only a few grains: three terrible things that happened to me in the days of
my tender childhood. First, a sore broke out on my face, in the flesh only, and the sore spread from one side to the
other, so that I was in great danger, almost beyond hope; and the Lord "sent His word and healed" me (Ps. 107:20), without
leaving any mark of injury on my face, and no scar at all. Second, a leprous boil rose on my member and closed the opening
of the urine for some time, so that it caused my parents worry, grief and much sighing over me. Third, a heavy boil covered
my whole leg, like the boil of Job, with ugly sufferings.

From all these the Lord saved me — besides other evil and lasting illnesses that come to all children, such as smallpox
and measles, and the cutting of teeth. Above all I was very prone to swelling of the tonsils, to catarrh and cough, and to
burning of the urine, and sometimes to small blisters and red spots. And besides the blows "with which I was wounded in
the house of my friends" (Zech. 13:6) — the teachers into whose hands I was given to learn, who were for the most part
cruel and beat me without pity — and besides other pains and ailments that passed over me from my earliest years: "many
a time have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me" (Ps. 129:2) ⟨S: two words, perhaps
"to destroy …"⟩ — from the falling out of teeth and the growing of others in their place, from the pressing of the
fingernails and the like, they are too many to number.

ואחר שבאתי קצת לכלל דעת, הרגשתי בצערו של אבא, יסוריו ועלבונו הנ"ל, שקמו עליו לקפח פרנסתו ולהורידו מכבודו. אחר זאת נפל אמ"ה ז"ל בחולי כבד ומסום (פלערוס) מתגבורת הירוקה, שנתעלל בסבת המחלוקת באלטונא, וכבר נתייאשו הרופאים ממנו, והתעניתי אני ואחיותי ב"ה בשבוע אחד, ואני עודני נער בן י"ב שנה [א]. ]וכאשר נתקבל אבי[ לרב בק"ק אשכנזים דאמשטרדם, והתחיל הגלות והטלטול שלי בכלל. בית אבא נסעו בסוף ימי החורף שנת ת"ע, והיתה עת הפשרת שלגים, שנפלו לרוב מאד בחורף העז והעצום ההוא, והיינו באחריות גדול על הדרך, כמעט חשבה העגלה שישבנו עליה כל הנשים וילדים להשבר, ולפול במים שגברו עליה, ובאו מים עד נפש. עלתה שאגתנו למרום, לולי ה' שהושיע לנו, אזי המים ישטפונו, נחלה עבר על ראשנו. באנו לחיים ולשלום אל ארץ אחרת, מדינת הולאנד, אשר לא ידענו תמול שלשום, אויר חדש, מנהגי עולם חדש. וכמה תמורות עברו עלינו, עד שהורגלנו בטבע המדינה, עם היות המאכלים ומשקים לא היו נאותים לנו כפי הרגלנו. ועל כולם לא ארכה השלוה, לא זאת המנוחה הניחו לעיף, כי מיד התחילו הקטטות והרדיפות של שני כתות החזקים המסופר למעלה, שכל אחת רצתה לבלוע חברתה חיים. אמ"ה לחץ ביניהם, כי באשר לא יכול להשוותם, ולא היה אפשר להצדיקם גם שתיהן, ובהגינו על צד החלוש שלא יהיה למרמס, קדשו עליו מלחמה וימררהו ורובו בעלי חצים הצד המתנגד, חשבו להוריד לארץ כבודו כנ"ל, וה' עזרו והיה מגן בעדו, ובעת ההיא עדת הספרדים החזיקו בידו. בכל זאת היתה עת צרה ליעקב ומבוכה מצערו של אבא; נוסף לזה שהרבה תורה בטלה המחלוקת הזאת. ואני בעת ההיא נעשיתי בר מצוה, את נשף חשקי אור לי"ד שם לי לחרדה [ב], מעוף צוקה וחשכה עת דאגה ויגון ואנחה, ולא היה הזמן גורם לשקוד על הספר, ולקנות שלמות מחסרון רב וחבר, מנהיג ומנהל לעשות אתי ברכה. ולהעדר שלותי לא עלתה ארוכה, עד שגרמו עונות המקום ההוא, ובא לשם הנחש הצבוע

When I came a little to understanding, I felt my father's suffering, his afflictions and the insults mentioned above,
when they rose against him to cut off his living and bring him down from his honour. After this my father fell into a
severe and dangerous illness (pleurisy) from an excess of bile, brought on by the controversy in Altona, and the doctors
had already given up on him. I and my sisters, may they live, fasted for a week, and I was still a boy of twelve [a].

[When my father was received] as rabbi of the Ashkenazi community of Amsterdam, my exile and my wandering began. My
father's household set out at the end of the winter of 5470 [1710]. It was the time of the thaw, after very heavy snows
in that fierce and mighty winter, and we were in great danger on the road: the wagon in which all the women and children
sat almost broke and fell into the waters that overflowed it, and "the waters came even to the soul" (Jon. 2:6). Our cry
went up on high; "had it not been the Lord who was on our side, then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone
over our soul" (Ps. 124:2–4). We came alive and in peace to another land, the country of Holland, which we had not known
before: new air, the customs of a new world. Many changes passed over us until we grew used to the nature of the
country, for the food and drink did not suit us according to our habit.

And above all, the quiet did not last; "this is the rest, give rest to the weary" (Isa. 28:12) — that they did not
allow. For at once the quarrels and persecutions began of the two factions of the strong men ⟨S: corrected to "of the
cantors"⟩, told above, each of which wanted to swallow the other alive. My father was pressed between them. Since he
could not reconcile them, and it was impossible to find both in the right, and since he protected the weak side so that
it should not be trampled, the opposing side declared war on him; "they embittered him, and shot at him, the archers";
they thought to bring his honour down to the ground, as said. And the Lord helped him and was a shield for him, and at
that time the congregation of the Sephardim supported him.

With all this it was "a time of trouble for Jacob" and confusion, from my father's suffering; besides which this
controversy caused much neglect of Torah. At that time I became bar mitzvah: "the twilight that I longed for He has turned
into trembling for me" (Isa. 21:4) [b] — "distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish" (Isa. 8:22), a time of worry,
grief and sighing. The times did not let me be diligent at the book and acquire perfection, for great lack of a companion,
a leader and a guide to deal with me in blessing. And there was no remedy for my lack of quiet, until the sins of that
place brought it about, and there came there the hypocritical serpent

the abominable Ḥayon, who threw the whole world into confusion. The righteous man, my father, was driven into a heavy
war, to stand against the presumptuous and powerful Sephardim, who broke their old covenant of love with him and turned
into enemies, meddling in a quarrel that was not theirs, to cover the shame of their protector and the sin that hung on
the head of R. S. A. [a] ⟨S: "may the name of the wicked rot"⟩, as said. So my father was forced to move his home
from there, as told, and he bent his shoulder to wander again on the wings of exile, to hasten an escape for himself and
his household.

In the middle of the winter of 5474 [1714] he travelled to London for some weeks, and sent us, his household, by ship
across the sea to Emden. We lived there as strangers until after Passover, though the people of that small town did us
every honour and every kindness they could. The learned leader R. L. Emden, of blessed memory, wanted to give me his
daughter as a wife: a learned and intelligent maiden — truly there was none like her in all the land of Germany. He
wanted to settle a large dowry on me, for he was very rich and a man of Torah; and his daughter too longed to join herself
to Torah and to lineage. But for a reason known in the family my father would not agree and call the match good.

It was a great trial for me too, for I was already of understanding, and knew how to weigh things in the scales of right
judgement. It was not hidden from me that it was a very fitting match, the like of which was not to be found in the land
in every respect — in capital and wealth, and as a daughter of a good family — so that it looked to me like a very
straight road, by which I could easily reach the goal of perfection. I knew well that my father could give me nothing,
all the more since he could barely provide for himself and his household, moving about without knowing where he was
going; and the leader and his household loved me very much and truly pressed me to carry out their plan and gain their
wish in me. Even so, far be it from me, I did not want to grieve my father, though my own mind leaned towards not giving
up so fitting a thing. That blemish in the family was not a reason to reject it either, for it was not disqualifying in
itself, God forbid; all the great leaders of Germany had already married into that family, which excelled in kindness
and greatness; and such a match does not happen every day. Even so I did not reveal even what was in my heart. I submitted
and accepted my father's decision with love, and concluded that she was not from the Lord to be my wife, for I was
destined for a greater match than this in respect of family. But "trouble and anguish have found me" (Ps. 119:143), as I
will write with God's help. And that important woman mentioned above, who had longed for me and did not succeed, was still
ready to do me good a long time afterwards, when the Blessed One brought me to sit on the rabbinical seat of Emden.

There too there was talk of honourable matches with this and that leader of Vienna(?). But the Lord brought before me […],

היא השתדלה על זה בכל נפשה, וגמלה אתי חסד הרבה ועם אשתי ע"ה, וכל ב"ב היתה לה חבה יתרה כאחוה וקורבה עצמית כמש"ל.
מעמדן נסע אמ"ה ז"ל בטפולו גדול, כי היינו חמשה בנים וחמש בנות לאבי ולאמי ז"ל; כולנו נולדנו להם באלטונא, ובת אחת קטנה היא לבדה נשארה מהנולדים לאמ"ה ז"ל באמשטרדם שלא נתקיימו, גם הבת הזאת מתה בדרך; רק אחותי רחל היתה אז אצל חמיה בק"ק אייזן שטאט; ואחותה הגדולה עם אישה וילדיה היו ג"כ אצלינו בעת ההיא, ואמי הרבנית ז"ל היתה מעוברת, ועמנו משרת ומשרתת כפי ההכרח, באופן שהיינו צריכין לשאת עגלות גדולות מלאות, ובעלי מלחמות מצויים בדרכים. נתעכבנו בבית דודי ז"ל ימים אחדים. שם נתן ה' אל לבי להשיב ע"ד מהר"א כהשגותיו על תשובת אמ"ה ז"ל, שלא הי"ל לאמ"ה פנאי לעיין בהן בדרך נסיעתו, ואני פניתי לראות ולחקור ולהבין בדבר באותן הימים, ושם כתבתי חלק מסוים מתשובה זו, ראשונה שחברתי בעז"ה מלמודים, לא הגדתי ולא הראיתי לאמ"ה, עד היותו בברעסלוי; אז ראה מה שכתבתי והשבתי בעדו, וישרו דברי מאד בעיניו, ונשקני על ראשי, וקרא אלי המקרא: שפתים ישק וכו'. אחר עיכוב איזה שבועות בברלין, נסענו לבוא לברעסלוי, ובדרך הזה היה לנו אחריות גדול, בסבת חיילות של צבא מלחמה מדינת פרייסן, שעברו אז בדרך ההיא, אע"פ שהיתה חרב של שלוה היו הדרכים בחזקת סכנה, ולפעמים היינו מוכרחים לעמוד ולהתעכב באמצע הדרך, וקצתם פגשו ובקושי גדול נפטרנו מהם בשלום ותהי לנס. באנו לברעסלוי שילהי קיץ הנ"ל [א].

She worked for this with all her soul, and showed great kindness to me and to my wife, of blessed memory; and she had a
great affection for all my household, like brotherhood and close kinship, as I will write.

From Emden my father set out with his large household. We were five sons and five daughters to my father and mother, of
blessed memory; we were all born to them in Altona, and of the children born to my father in Amsterdam, who did not
survive, only one little daughter was left; and this daughter too died on the way. Only my sister Rachel was then with her

rebbetzin, of blessed memory, was pregnant; and there were with us a manservant and a maidservant, as necessary. So we
needed to load ⟨S: "two"⟩ large wagons, full; and men of war were about on the roads. We stayed some days in my uncle's
house ⟨S: "and after several adventures we came to Berlin; and it was then a time of war between kingdoms"⟩.

There the Lord put it into my heart to answer the objections of R. A. ⟨S: corrected to "R. M."⟩ to my father's
responsum, for my father had no time to study them on his journey. In those days I set myself to look into the matter,
to search it out and understand it, and there I wrote a certain part of this responsum, the first that I composed, with
God's help, out of my studies. I did not tell my father or show it to him until he was in Breslau. Then he saw what I had
written and answered on his behalf, and my words were very right in his eyes; he kissed me on my head and recited to me
the verse, "He kisses the lips", and so on.

After a stay of some weeks in Berlin we set out for Breslau. On this road we were in great danger because of the soldiers
of the army of the land of Prussia, who were then passing along that road; although it was a time of peace, the roads
were considered dangerous, and sometimes we had to stop and wait in the middle of the road. Some of them met us, and with
great difficulty we got away from them in peace, and it was a miracle. We came to Breslau at the end of the said summer

From Breslau we set out for Poland at the beginning of the winter of 5475 [1714]. My father married off my sister Neḥamah,

that the doctors too did not understand the nature of my illness. After many years in which this strange ailment
afflicted me, I felt that it came from an excess of blood, which needed to be lightened in me; so it did not let go of
me until the "golden vein" opened for me, with God's help, and then it left me a little. Only there [melancholy] grew
strong on me, and I was prone to the black humour. I travelled to Hamburg in this distress and stayed there until the
rainy season was over; and at the beginning of the summer my father went back with me from Hamburg to Breslau and made
my wedding [a] ⟨S: "on the way the customs took from me the little money they had given me …"⟩.

After my wedding, time separated me from my father; I never had the merit to see him again. Parting from him was as hard
for me as the parting of the soul from the body ⟨S: a long note, mostly read: "and with all this I did not taste any taste(?), not even the taste of intercourse; joy and gladness were taken from me … on the way to Breslau. I did not taste the taste of joy, for I was … grief and sighing from the black bile"⟩ — above all because I was a boy of seventeen, and tender, and lacked the perfection I longed for; and I
had not taken from my father and teacher even as much as a dog laps from the sea, in the hard times that passed over me
at the beginning of my growing up, as said, most of which went by in sorrow, grief and sighing, wandering and moving from
land to land for a long time. Now my face was set towards a land I had not known before, to live in the country of
Moravia, among a people and a language I did not know, and customs of the country I was not used to.

And above all, my heart was troubled within me that I had not been worthy to serve my father as I should. For in my
childhood and youth I said in my heart, there is still time; so "I did not listen to the voice of my teachers, nor
incline my ear to my instructors" (Prov. 5:13). And when I did want and desire to learn, I found no master, teacher or
guide. My father was mostly occupied in the hard war, as said; nor could he keep teachers for his young sons at home by
themselves, especially as living in a great city like Amsterdam is hard; and he accepted no gifts and presents, so the
money was gone from his vessels. So I, in my early youth, at about fifteen, had to teach my two little brothers — not
only did I myself have no teacher or instructor any longer, but it was not in his power to keep for them a special
teacher who would be right in his eyes.

When I parted from my father, I travelled with my wife and my father-in-law, of blessed memory, to the land of Moravia.
When we arrived, tired and weary from the road, in the first year of the joy of my wedding, the plague spread in the land
of Moravia, and came also to the town of Brod, the town in which we lived, just after my father-in-law had come home and
had hardly settled in his house. After a few days the plague began among the people. We fled the town and moved out to
the villages to find escape, and we were cast out on the face of the field. In the winter days we had to lodge under a
tent spread in the forest, in the frost of the night,

for several weeks, until by the Lord's mercy the villagers' compassion was stirred and they let us come into the

When this trouble had passed, I saw a new world, a new nature and new customs. In my father-in-law's house, too, the
living was hard at that time, and I had to make do with the barest necessities, against the tenderness of my nature and
the habits I had learned in my father's house. And at once I tasted a taste more bitter than death, for my wife, of
blessed memory, was hard and stubborn, though she was gentle in speech and lovely; only my sins did this to me. Besides,
"when the barley is finished from the jar, strife comes knocking at the house" [a] in my father-in-law's house; and
they "ploughed with my heifer to find out my riddle" (Judg. 14:18) — the place where I had hidden my purse, the little
money I had received. I did not agree to give an outlet for the money and throw coins away for nothing; and they made
quarrels with me and almost separated me from my wife, so that I had no rest, no quiet and no peace.

Never in my life did I sit one day in tranquillity. When the flower of my youth blossomed, "from the womb of the morning,
the dew of my youth" (Ps. 110:3), the days of my boyhood and youth passed in poverty; all the times came in sorrow,
trouble and suffering; "from within and without my sighs are many" (Lam. 1:22), and all my joy was darkened (Isa. 24:11).
With all this, "the precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart" (Ps. 19:9), the broken and contrite heart; they
were to me the joy of my heart and the restoring of my soul: "unless Your law had been my delight, I should then have
perished in my affliction" (Ps. 119:92). Only the main thing was missing: books. I had then only the four Ṭurim, which
I had brought with me, given me by my uncle ⟨S: "a gift"⟩, of blessed memory, as a wedding present. In them I
studied, as the good hand of the Lord was upon me, according to my understanding; besides them I did not have even a
volume of the Gemara as I wished, except on loan and with great difficulty. Though my father-in-law, of blessed memory,
had several sets of the Talmud, and his house was full of precious and honoured books, my eye had no access to them, and
I had no permission to take any of them to study as I needed.

With all this pressure and want, young men of desire at once set their eyes on me: scholars married and unmarried longed
to study with me. I wanted more to learn than to teach; even so I could not make their word and their pressing void and
refuse them, God forbid, also because I said: "from my students more than from all" (b. Ta'anit 7a) — they will keep my
learning in my hands. So I bent my shoulder and became "a servant under tribute" (Gen. 49:15), serving the service of the
Lord with companions who listened to my voice. Young men of the people and important scholars gathered to me, and I
studied with them Gemara, Rashi and Tosafot, the Ṭur Oraḥ Ḥayyim with the Beit Yosef, Bible, halakhah and aggadah; my
words were sweet to those who heard them, and their company was pleasant and agreeable to me, good fellowship. They even
wanted to provide the needs of my household amply, for their fathers were rich merchants, notables of the land
Kahana's notes

[a] After the saying of the Sages (b. Bava Metzia 59a): "When the barley is finished from the jar, strife comes knocking
at the house."


הגר, ולא אביתי כלל, ועד בשחק נאמן כי לא לקחתי כסף ושוה כסף כל מאומה.
אבל לא ארכו לי ימי המנוחה והשמחה, כי בעוד שלש שנים כשני שכיר, שהייתי שכיר יום, כי לא הנחתי אותם מלפני לצאת ידי שמועה מפי פ"א בלבד, אבל היו חוזרים על תלמודם לפני, ביחוד בלמודי שיעורי דרבנן הפוסקים טור עם ב"י, לא נפטרו מאתי עד שהיה שגור בפיהם, מה ששמעו וקבלו דבר יום ביומו, ולפעמים הייתי טורח עמהם כל כך, עד שיגעתי בקראי נחר גרוני, והוצרכתי לקשור ראשי בסודר מרוב עבודה כדי להסביר להם ולהסדיר למודם בפיהם, שיהא ערוך בלב ושמור בלשון בלי משגה ובלי טעות בהבנה, פתאום שודד בא אהלי וכל מיתרי נתקו, זמותי עברו מורשי לבבי, פלצות בעתתני רעדה אחזתני, את נשף חשקי שם לי לחרדה, בבוא אלי שמועת פטירת אמ"ה ז"ל, ההפך עלי בלהות נהפך עלי הגלגל, גלגלני לאחור צנפני כדור אל ארץ רחבת ידים, היא מדינת פולין, הלכתי בדרך רחוקה אשר לא עברתי בה מתמול שלשום, עברתי יחידי עם אנשי פולין בטלטול הקשה, הרבה יותר ממאה פרסאות בסכנות רבות. פ"א ראינו בחוש, כי הלכנו מן המלון, נתלוו אלינו שודדים שני רוכבי סוסים, הלכו אצל עגלה שלנו עד היער, הלוך ושוב ומביטים אלינו כנועצים עלינו, עד שפגענו בעגלה אחרת של תגרים נכרים מזויינים שהלכו לפנינו, וכראות הרוכבים הנ"ל את העגלה ההיא נוסעת לפנינו, אז מיד חזרו לאחוריהם, ולא נגע בנו רע. ברוך המציל! ובאתי ת"ל לק' לבוב בשילהי קיץ תע"ח, ומצאתי בית אבי ז"ל מתאבלים אבל כבד גם כל הארץ בוכים על אבדתם היקרה בלי תמורה מאנו הנחם כנ"ל [א], ואנכי פתחתי פי להספידו מחדש, ודרשתי על קברו של אמ"ה ז"ל בפני קבוץ גדול שהיה, כי באו לשמוע אמרי כל יקירי נכבדי הקהל, והמון רב עמהם ליקרא דשכבא, ושמעו אמרי כי נעמו, וקניתי שם טוב מאד, כי היו הדברים נעימים מאד לאזני השומעים, וקראתי שם הדרוש „יציב פתגם", על שם העמדת המצבה שעשיתי לאמ"ה ז"ל על קברו בו ביום שדרשתי והספדתי עליו. ומענין זה של עשיית מצבה היה נושא הדרוש, וכלול בתוך פסוקי פרשת השבוע, בהמצאה רבה ועומק ומתיקות, ודברים מיושבים
[א] הגאון חכם צבי מת בליל יום ב' דר"ת אייר תע"ח, בן נ"ח שנה עיין בס' "יציב פתגם" ליעב"ץ (דף ט"ז ע"ב ודף כ"ו ע"ב).

of Hungary; and I would not at all. The faithful witness in the sky (Ps. 89:38) knows that I took no money or money's
worth of any kind.

But my days of rest and joy did not last. For within three years, "as the years of a hireling" (Isa. 16:14), in which I
was a day-labourer ⟨S: a five-line note, partly read: "diligent … as if I were …"⟩ — for I did not let them leave me
having heard a lesson from my mouth only once, but they repeated their learning before me, especially the lessons in the
rabbinic codes, the Ṭur with the Beit Yosef; they did not leave me until it was fluent in their mouths, what they had
heard and received day by day; and sometimes I toiled with them so much that "I am weary of my crying, my throat is dried"
(Ps. 69:4), and I had to bind my head with a cloth from the great labour, to explain to them and set their learning in
order in their mouths, so that it would be arranged in the heart and kept on the tongue, without mistake and without error
in understanding — suddenly "the spoiler came upon my tent, and all my cords are broken" (Jer. 10:20); "my purposes are
broken off, the thoughts of my heart" (Job 17:11); "horror has overwhelmed me, trembling has seized me; the twilight I
longed for He has turned into trembling for me" (Isa. 21:4), when the news of my father's death reached me. "Terrors are
turned upon me" (Job 30:15): the wheel turned upon me and rolled me backwards; "He will toss me like a ball into a large
country" (Isa. 22:18), the land of Poland.

I went on a long road on which I had never travelled before. I travelled alone with men of Poland, in hard wandering,
much more than a hundred leagues, in many dangers. Once we saw it plainly: as we left the inn, two robbers on horseback
joined us and rode beside our wagon as far as the forest, back and forth, looking at us as if plotting against us, until
we came upon another wagon, of armed gentile traders, going ahead of us. When the riders saw that wagon going before us
they turned back at once, and no evil touched us. Blessed is the Rescuer!

I came, thank God, to the holy community of Lwów at the end of the summer of 5478 [1718], and found my father's household
in heavy mourning, and the whole land weeping for its precious loss, which had no replacement, refusing to be comforted,
as said [a]. I opened my mouth to lament him anew, and preached at my father's grave before a great gathering; for all
the dear and honoured men of the community came to hear my words, and a great multitude with them, in honour of the dead.
They heard my words, for they were pleasant, and I won a very good name, for the words were very pleasant to the ears of
the hearers. I called the sermon Yatziv Pitgam, after the setting up of the gravestone that I made for my father on his
grave on the very day I preached and lamented him. The subject of the sermon was this making of a gravestone, woven into
the verses of the weekly portion with much invention, depth and sweetness, and well-settled words

היטב הדק, באופן שהכירו כולם שהיה הדרוש מן החדש, חדושי תורה שלא שמעתן אוזן, ומכוונים הנושא עם פרשת השבוע בדיוק נמרץ; המה הרהיבוני לחברו בקונטרס מיוחד, וכבר בא לדפוס בעזה"י.
גם שם לא חדלתי מלתת מתקי ותנובתי, כי למדתי עם אחי הצעירים הבחורים, גם עם חתן הרב ר"ל ר"י בעת ההיא בלבוב, והוא היה בן הרב ר' בצלאל אחי חמי הרב, שהיה אב"ד באוסטרא, ובנו הלז היה אחר זאת ר"י באוסטרא. ק"ק לבוב כבדוני בעת ההיא להיות לראש ב"ד שלהם, ובבר היו רוצים לקבלני לרב ואב"ד, אם היה לי חתימת זקן. כל כך היתה אהבתם עזה תקועה בלבם ושמורה לבית אמ"ה ז"ל, כי אמרו בניו ודאי ילכו בדרכיו, אך עדיין הייתי רך בשנים, כי רוב שנים יודיעו חכמה, והייתי שפל אנשים, אם גדול הייתי בעיני כל העם, לא בא במחשבתי לחזר ולבקש אחר שום גדולה וכבוד; רק מרוב תוקף אהבה עזה וחבה יתירה עשו זאת לתת לי מעטה תהלה וכבוד רב"ד, שהיא סמוכה לרב אב"ד, וחשבו שאתיישב אצלם לקבוע דירתי בלבוב, ובל בני הקהלה היו מתברכים בי ובבית אבי, הלואי שיתקיימו בי הברכות ששמעו אזני מאחרי. בכל פעם שהייתי עובר ברחוב, ושם יושבות נשים בחנויות מוכרות סחורות מאכלים ומשקים, היו מתברכות בנו בעברנו דרך שם. גם הרב הקדוש ר"ח רייציש הי"ד [א] נתן עיניו בי להחזיקני שם, בקש ממני שאקבע דירתי בלבוב, כדי ללמוד עם אחיו חתנו הרב הקדוש הי"ד; גם הקצינים המפורסמים הרבנים כמו' העניך וגיסו ר' נתן ע"ה רצו שאתיישב בזאלקווי ואלמוד בבה"מ שלהם, ולעשות לי הספקה טובה.
אמת כבר הייתי מרוצה לקבוע דירתי בלבוב, בראותי רוב החבה עצומה וגודל הכבוד של בית אבא וארץ טובה ורחבת ידים לפנינו, הן בענין הפרנסה בזול, והן בענין שידוכים הגונים המצוים לבנים ובנות עוד קטנים. כי עם היות שהניח אמ"ה ז"ל שבעה יתומים קטנים, ארבעה בנים ושלש בנות, אלמלא היינו להוטים אחר ממון היו מעשירים אותנו, באשר כל קציני ארץ פולין היו רוצים להתדבק בזרעו של אמ"ה ז"ל ולהפריז להם מוהר ומתן כחפצנו, גם לתת דורונות גדולות לאמי הרבנית ע"ה, ואפילו אם היו לנו שבעים בנים להשיאן לא היו מספיקין למלא תשוקת כל פני הארץ, החפצים בבני אמ"ה ז"ל; ולא לבד שלא

ground very fine, so that everyone recognised that the sermon was new — Torah novellae that no ear had heard — and that
its subject matched the weekly portion with great precision. They urged me to set it down as a separate pamphlet, and it
has already come out in print, with God's help.

There too I did not cease to give "my sweetness and my good fruit" (Judg. 9:11). I studied with my young brothers, the
youths, and also with the bridegroom, the rabbi R. L., head of a yeshivah, who was in Lwów at that time. He was the son of
the rabbi R. Bezalel, brother of my father-in-law the rabbi, who was head of the court in Ostróg; and this son of his was
afterwards head of the yeshivah in Ostróg.

The holy community of Lwów honoured me at that time by making me head of their court; and they would already have wanted
to receive me as rabbi and head of the court, had I had a full beard. So strong was their love, fixed in their hearts and
kept for my father's house; for they said, his sons will surely walk in his ways. But I was still young in years — "the
multitude of years should teach wisdom" (Job 32:7) — and I was the lowliest of men, though I was great in the eyes of all
the people. It did not enter my mind to seek or pursue any greatness or honour. Only out of the strength of their great
love and affection did they do this, to give me a mantle of praise and the honour of judge of the court, which is next to
rabbi and head of the court; and they thought that I would settle with them and make my home in Lwów. All the members of
the community blessed themselves by me and by my father's house — would that the blessings my ears heard behind me were
fulfilled in me. Every time I passed through the street where women sat in shops selling goods, food and drink, they
blessed themselves by us as we went by.

The holy rabbi R. Ḥ. Reitzes, may God avenge his blood [a], also set his eyes on me to keep me there, and asked me to
make my home in Lwów, in order to study with his brother, his son-in-law, the holy rabbi, may God avenge his blood. The
famous leaders, the learned R. Henikh and his brother-in-law R. Nathan, of blessed memory, also wanted me to settle in
Żółkiew and study in their house of study, and to make good provision for me.

Truly, I was already content to make my home in Lwów, seeing the great affection and the great honour for my father's
house, and a good and wide land before us — both in the cheapness of living and in the fitting matches to be found for
the sons and daughters, who were still small. For although my father left seven young orphans, four sons and three
daughters, had we been eager for money they would have made us rich: all the leaders of the land of Poland wanted to join
themselves to my father's descendants and to settle on them dowry and gift as we pleased, and also to give great presents
to my mother the rebbetzin. Even if we had had seventy sons to marry off, they would not have been enough to satisfy the
longing of the whole land, which desired my father's sons. And not only would we not
