אותה, לא רצה לקחתה, ותבחר מחנק נפשו מקרוב אליה; עכ"ז השיאוהו ויכלו לו אנשי שלומו כי אמרו לו אין אחר מעשה כלום, ואם לא יקחנה ברצון סופו ליקח באונס ובכפיה, או כל הון ביתו יתן בעד הבושה לבת ישראל שלא חטאה לו, והי"ל לחקור תחלה, איהו דאפסיד אנפשיה ונסתפחה שדהו, ע"כ מוטב שלא יכניס עצמו בזילותא דב"ד בחנם, כי לא יזכה בדין ולכן יזכה במקחו; פתוהו ויפת לקיים השידוך, ועיילא ליה תרקבא דדינרי לאוקמיה ברבנות דק' קידאן, דהיינו ישכר עשה חילוף עם רי"ח, שהיה אז אב"ד בקידאן, והתנה עמו שיעשה הוא לו כל האפשרות מצדו, להשתדל בעבורו לקבלו לרי"ח לאב"ד דג"ק, נגד זה ימסור לו רי"ח הרבנות דקידאן, שעמד לרי"ח ג"כ בכסף מלא, וקבל עליו ישכר כהן לשלם אותו סך ממון שהיו חייבים ק' קידאן לרי"ח, ושיעשה הוא עמו בטובה להשיג הרבנות לפני חתנו של ישכר, כדי שלא יצטרכו בני קידאן לשלם המעות לרי"ח, אך אז יוסיף להם ישכר עוד איזה סך הלואה. על דרך זה ובאופן הלז נגמר דבר החליפין; בצירוף איזה חיזוק לדבר שעשו ישכר כהן מצד אחד, להעיד על רי"ח שיצא לו שם בכל מדינת ליטא שהוא גדול מרבן; באשר ישכר היה סוחר למדינת ליטא ומכיר קצת אנשים שם, ובג"ק לא נודע דבר החליפין של הרבנות הנ"ל, ובהיות ישכר פשוט מוחזק לנאמן, חשבו אנשי הג"ק שאמת הדבר נכון בפיו, שרי"ח אדם גדול מפורסם באותה מדינה, והאמינו שכך הוא כמו שהגדיל שמו כ' ישכר, שלא חשדוהו במאומה ולא עלה ע"ד אדם דבר אחר, רק לשם שמים הוא עושה, לטובת הג"ק לזכותם באדם גדול כזה, שאין על עפר משלו לפי דבריו בכל מילי מעליותא, א"כ להנאת עצמו דרש טובת בתו. ורי"ח עשה המצאה שלו מצד אחר, לפרסם שמו בג"ק אשר לא ידעו ממנו מאומה. ככה ספרו היודעים האמת, כד שלח ציר מיוחד למדן או מלמד ממדינת ליטא מאוהביו ומיודעיו, מי יודע כמה שכר פסק לו, וצרור הכסף נתן בידו, לפזר אל הלומדים שבג"ק, וביחוד אל המלמדים המצוים כאן מאנשי פולין ומליטא, כי על פיהם יהיה כל ריב וכל נגע בקהלות אשכנז, כי בכל פעם שעוסקים אשכנזים בקבלת רב חדש, מתאוים דווקא לרחוקים אשר לא ידעו ולא הכירו מעולם, באשר ע"פ הרוב הקרובים אליהם אינם חשובים בעיניהם; ביחוד מאחר שהממונים לקבל רב חדש, אינם לומדים ואינן בקיאים ברבנים, ולא הכרה והבחנה בין טוב לרע, מוכרחים לשאול את פי אחרים, אנשים נכרים מארץ רחוקה בפולין וליטא, ונמלכים במלמדים שלהם השכיחים אצלם, כסבורים שיכולין לסמוך עליהן כי

her, he did not want to take her, "and his soul chose strangling" (Job 7:15) rather than come near her. For all that, they married him off; "his
friends prevailed against him" (cf. Obad. 1:7), for they told him that after the deed nothing can be done, and if he did not take her willingly he
would in the end take her by force and compulsion, or give all the wealth of his house for the shame of a daughter of Israel who had not sinned
against him; he should have inquired first — "he has lost, and his field is diminished" (cf. b. Ketubot 76b); so it is better that he not bring
himself to the disgrace of the court for nothing, for he would not win at law, and so he should be content with his bargain. They persuaded him, and
he was persuaded, to carry out the match; and "a bag of dinars was brought in to him" to set him up in the rabbinate of the community of Keidan.

That is: Issachar made an exchange with R. Y[eḥezkel], who was then head of the court in Keidan. He stipulated with him that he would do all that
was possible on his side to work for his acceptance, R. Y[eḥezkel], as head of the court of the Three Communities; in return R. Y[eḥezkel] would hand
over to him the rabbinate of Keidan, which had also cost R. Y[eḥezkel] full money; and Issachar Kohen undertook to pay the sum of money that the
community of Keidan owed R. Y[eḥezkel], and R. Y[eḥezkel] would do him the favour of obtaining the rabbinate for Issachar's son-in-law, so that the
people of Keidan would not have to pay the money to R. Y[eḥezkel]; and then Issachar would add for them some further sum as a loan. In this way and
this manner the exchange was concluded — together with some support for the matter that Issachar Kohen made on one side, testifying that R.
Y[eḥezkel] had a name in all the country of Lithuania as a great man, "greater than a rabban"; for Issachar was a merchant to the country of Lithuania
and knew some people there. In the Three Communities the exchange of the rabbinate was not known; and since Issachar was a simple man held to be
trustworthy, the people of the Three Communities thought that the thing was true and established in his mouth, that R. Y[eḥezkel] was a great and
famous man in that country, and believed that it was as R. Issachar magnified his name. They suspected him of nothing, and it entered no one's mind
otherwise than that he was acting for the sake of Heaven, for the good of the Three Communities, to grant them so great a man, "who upon earth has
not his like" (cf. Job 41:25), according to his words, in every excellent matter — when in fact he sought the good of his daughter for his own
benefit.

And R. Y[eḥezkel] made his own contrivance on another side, to make his name known in the Three Communities, which knew nothing of him. So those who
know the truth told: he sent a special envoy, a scholar or teacher from the country of Lithuania, one of his friends and acquaintances — who knows
what fee he fixed for him — and put "the bundle of money" in his hand, to scatter among the scholars in the Three Communities, and especially among
the teachers who are found here, people from Poland and Lithuania; for "by their word shall every controversy and every stroke be" (Deut. 21:5) in
the communities of Germany. For whenever the Ashkenazim are busy accepting a new rabbi, they long precisely for distant ones whom they have never
known or recognised, since for the most part those near them are not esteemed in their eyes; especially since those appointed to accept a new rabbi
are not learned and are not expert in rabbis, and have no knowledge or discrimination between good and evil; they must ask the mouth of others,
strangers from a distant land, Poland and Lithuania, and take counsel with their teachers, who are frequent among them, thinking that they can rely
on them, since


אוכלי לחמם הם; אך רובן של מלמדים בארץ אשכנז, לטובתן ולהנאתן, דורשים לשבח הרב ההוא אשר הכין לבבם ופיהם לספר בשבחו, ע"י שמלא ידם לכהן לו, והם יועצים לפי דרכם לבעלי בתים השואלים אותם, ע"ד הרבנים המפורסמים לשבח בארצם, והללו המסודרים לקבלת הרב, נותנים דעתם לאותם שיעצום המלמדים; ויהי בהגיע תור קבלת הרב בג"ק, הלך איש עתי הנ"ל והקדים עצמו לבוא לכאן, לקנות אוהבים לרי"ח בזהובים, בכסף מלא קנה אותם, בפרט המלמדים אשר לא ידעוהו מלפנים, השתדל עמהם שיאמרו בשמו דברי חידושי תורה ערבים כפי שיודעים, ופשטים נעימים שבידיהם משם גדולי ארץ, ושילמדו עם תלמידיהם בכל הענינים שיאמרו בשבת פשט על שלחן אביהם לומר ד"ת במנהג ישראל באשכנז, והיה המלמד ברצי כסף מוכר הכזב, מזבין מילי בדינרי, ולומד עם נעריו איזה פשט נאה, שיודע ושקבל בשם גדולי הדור אשר מלפנים בישראל, והוא משגירו בפיהם על שם רי"ח, בתואר והדר לו כאלו ממנו יצא, כלבושים הלל לבושו, וכאשר בא הנער לדבר על שולחנו של אביו, להשמיע באזניו חדוש שלמד בשבוע זו, היה מרים בכח קולו בהתלהבות גדולה בלשון הזה: דבר זה אמר רבינו ה' ר' יחזקאל קצינלנבוגן רב דקידאן, וכך היו עושין רבים מהמלמדים אשר התרפס להם, והכסף יענה את הקול, עד שהוציאו [על רי"ח קול] גדול בג"ק, כי היו אומרים משמו דברים מתוקים וחריפים, ובשבח עצום בהפלגה גדולה, באופן זה גנבו דעת האנשים, [ואם שאלו את פי] המלמדים, אם ידעו את האיש אם שיחו נאה אם הגון הוא לרבנות דג"ק, היו משיבים פשיטא יחיד בדורו, לא הניח כמותו בתורה בחכמה וחסידות, בלשון צח ובכל המעלות ומדות שמנו חכמים אין לו חבר בעולם, [שכלו אין] לאדם לעמוד עליו, אם לא יתענה רי"ח תחלה משבת לשבת להחליש כח שכלו כדי שלא יעמיקו כל כך בהמצאותיו, [והשומע יתענה להחליש כח גופו] ולמעט חלבו ודמו לזכך החומר שלו, למען יהא שכלו דק ומוכשר לקבל, ולירד לסוף דעתו של רי"ח. כולי האי ואולי.
אלה קצות דרכי מלמדים, בתשובות לשואליהם ההולכים לתומם, וסמכו עליהם כעורים נמשכים אחריהם, והמה לא ראו ולא ידעו את האיש רי"ח, רק הכסף יענה את הקול. סוף דבר גרם העון שבא זה האיש לישב בראש דג"ק. כד רגיז רעיא על ענא, פרנס לפי הדור. מצא [אלטונא] כג"ע לפניו ואחריו מדבר שממה כמש"ל. וכשהלכו פני העיר לקראתו להקביל פניו בשמחה, לראות פני אדוניהם החדש, אשר היו מצפים להנות מאורו, אור חדש כמו שאמרו המלמדים המעידים

they eat their bread. But most of the teachers in the land of Germany, for their own good and benefit, preach the praise of that rabbi who has
"prepared their heart" and their mouth to tell his praise, by having "filled their hand to minister to him as priests" (cf. Ex. 28:41); and they
advise, after their manner, the householders who ask them about the rabbis famous for praise in their country, and those charged with accepting the
rabbi set their minds on those whom the teachers advised.

When the turn came for accepting the rabbi in the Three Communities, the said "fit man" (Lev. 16:21) went and came here in advance, to buy friends
for R. Y[eḥezkel] with gold pieces; for full money he bought them, especially the teachers who had not known him before. He worked with them that they
should repeat in his name pleasant Torah novellae, as they knew, and agreeable interpretations they had in hand in the name of the great men of the
land; and that they should study with their pupils, in all the matters ⟨S: a letter, "m"(?)⟩, what they would say on the Sabbath, an interpretation at
their fathers' table — to speak words of Torah, as is the custom of Israel in Germany. And the teacher, "for pieces of silver" (Ps. 68:31), selling
lies, "selling words for dinars", would teach his boys some fine interpretation that he knew and had received in the name of the great men of the
generation of old in Israel, and he put it in their mouths in the name of R. Y[eḥezkel], with title and splendour, as if it had come from him —
"garments, such as Hillel's are his garments". And when the boy came to speak at his father's table, to make him hear a novella he had learned that
week, he would lift up his voice with force, with great fervour, in these words: "This thing our master the rabbi R. Yeḥezkel Katzenellenbogen, rabbi
of Keidan, said." And so did many of the teachers whom he had bribed, "and money answers the voice" (cf. Eccl. 10:19), until they put out [a great
report about R. Y[eḥezkel]] in the Three Communities, for they repeated in his name sweet and sharp things, with enormous and excessive praise. In this
way they stole the people's minds. [And if they asked] the teachers whether they knew the man and his talk (2 Kgs. 9:11), whether he was fit for the
rabbinate of the Three Communities, they would answer: "Obviously, unique in his generation! He has not left his like in Torah, in wisdom and piety,
in elegant language and in all the virtues and qualities the sages listed; he has no companion in the world; [his intelligence no] man can grasp,
unless R. Y[eḥezkel] first fasts from Sabbath to Sabbath to weaken the power of his intelligence, so that they need not go so deep into his
inventions; [and the hearer should fast to weaken the strength of his body] and lessen his fat and blood, to refine his matter, so that his intellect
may be fine and fit to receive, and to reach the depth of R. Y[eḥezkel]'s mind." So much — and perhaps!

"These are but the outskirts of the ways" (Job 26:14) of teachers, in their answers to those who ask them and "go in their simplicity" (2 Sam. 15:11),
and rely on them, drawn after them like the blind; and they had not seen nor known the man R. Y[eḥezkel] — only "money answers the voice". In the
end sin caused this man to come and sit at the head of the Three Communities: "when the shepherd is angry with the flock", a parnas according to the
generation (cf. b. Arakhin 17a). He found [Altona] "as the garden of Eden before him, and behind him a desolate wilderness" (Joel 2:3), as written
above. And when the leading men of the town went out to meet him and greet him with joy, to see the face of their new lord, from whose light they
hoped to benefit, "a new light", as the teachers who testified said,


בשכרם, אמר להם איזה ד"ת ולא הבינו דבורו כלל, כי בלעגי שפה ובלשון אחרת מדבר, נלעג לשון אין בינה ממש בלי גוזמא, אנכי היודע ועד כי כ"פ דבר עמי, וכבר ישב פה הרבה יותר משלשים שנה, ולא הבינותי מאמרו ולשונו לגמרי, עאכ"ו בתחלת בואו הנה מעם עמקי שפה מארץ ליטא, לכן חלו פניו שיכתוב להם החידוש שאמר להם, אולי יבינוהו מתוך הכתב, ולא יכלו כי היה בעיניהם כדברי הספר החתום, גם מצד הכתיבה השחורה שלא נראית כמוה לרוע, ולא היה באפשרות לאדם לקרותו, כמו דבורו הבלתי מובן כצפצוף, והן מצד הלשון ג"כ לא ניתן לקרות, אפילו מביני מדע בשלשת דברים הללו, ר"ל: כתב, דבור, לשון; היה יחיד בדורו בלי ספק, חוץ מן המעלות המדותיות כמש"ל, ועל כן בראותם שגם מתוך הכתב לא יכלו להשיג החדוש של ד"ת שהיו חושקים לזכות בו, ולידע ולהבין שמץ דבר מכל ההפלגה הגדולה ששבחוהו וקלסוהו המלמדים, אשר נתנו עידיהן אידיהן ויצדקו, בקשו למלמדים העומדים עליו, אשר היו קצת צחי לשון יותר ממנו, ודבורם מובן ויודעי ספר המכירים בכתבו ובלשונו, לקרות לפניהם ולתרגם להם מה שכתב להם רבם החדש, וקראוהו אבל לא מצאו חזון הקוראים, והשומעים לא זכו להבין כלום, ונתקיים קצת מהבטחה הנ"ל, כי אולי מפני שלא התענה, או התענה יותר מדאי, או שלא התענו תחלה השומעים והקוראים דבריו, לא זכו לכך. ובאמת אפילו אם היו חובטים ראשם, לא יכלו להבינו כי אין תבונה בו, גם מצד הענין אין דעת אדם מבין סובלו.
אך מה שנעשה נעשה. דבר המלך, דלא עביד דינא בלא דינא, אין להשיב, כי כך נגזר עליהם כמש"ל, יען מאסו את מי השלוח, עונותיהם עשו זאת שהקים ה' עליהם רועה לרעות את עצמו, ואת הצאן לא רעה אותם דעה והשכל, כי אם התול בד"ת ולעג בלומדיה, מן אז והלאה גבר ההפקר בע"ה, מחוץ חרבו תשכל, והק' רב"ך התקיף הגדול הנ"ל, היה נוח לו מאד ברב כזה, כי היה נשמע לו לכל מה שהיה מבין רי"ח ומכיר בין ריסי עיניו של רב"ך, והיה קורא: זידע, ר"ל זקני, כך קורין בלשון פולניא לאבי האב: זידע, וכשהיו מבקשין ממנו דבר בעסקי הקהל ויחידים, היה חוקר ודורש תחלה ושואל: מה זידע אומר בדבר הזה, ועל פיו מה שהיה, שהודיעוהו דעתו חפצו ורצונו של רב"ך היה עושה, ולא היה משגיח כלל על אחרים, בין ייטיב להם או ירע לא איכפת לו, רק שיכשרו מעשיו בעיני העשיר הזקן וגבר אלם הנ"ל, בזה היה נזהר בכל יכלתו, למען ימצא חן בעיניו ובעיני בניו וחתניו אוהביו ומיודעיו, שהיו כולם ברום מעלה

for their reward, he said some words of Torah to them, and they did not understand his speech at all, for "with stammering lips and another
tongue" (Isa. 28:11) he spoke, "of a stammering tongue that you cannot understand" (Isa. 33:19), truly without exaggeration. I know and am
witness: he spoke with me many times, and he had already lived here much more than thirty years, and I did not understand his speech and language
completely — how much more at the beginning of his coming here from a people "of deep speech" (Isa. 33:19) from the land of Lithuania. So they
entreated him to write for them the novella he had told them; perhaps they would understand it from the writing. But they could not, for it was in
their eyes "as the words of a book that is sealed" (Isa. 29:11) — both because of the black handwriting, whose like for badness has not been seen,
and which no man could read, like his speech, unintelligible as chirping; and because of the language too it could not be read, even by men of
understanding. In these three things, that is: writing, speech, language, he was unique in his generation without doubt — apart from the moral
virtues, as written above.

So when they saw that even from the writing they could not grasp the novella of Torah that they longed to gain, and to know and understand a whiff
of anything of all the great exaggeration with which the teachers had praised and extolled him, who "brought their witnesses, that they might be
justified" (Isa. 43:9), they asked the teachers who attended him, who were somewhat more fluent of tongue than he, whose speech was intelligible
and who knew books and recognised his handwriting and language, to read before them and translate for them what their new rabbi had written. They
read it, but the readers found no vision (cf. Hos. 12:11), and the hearers did not merit to understand anything. So something of the said promise
was fulfilled: perhaps because he had not fasted, or had fasted too much, or because the hearers and readers of his words had not fasted first, they
did not merit it. In truth, even if they had beaten their heads, they could not have understood it, for "there is no understanding in him" (Deut.
32:28); and in substance too, no man's mind can understand and bear it.

But what is done is done. "The word of the king" — who does not judge without justice — cannot be answered, for so it was decreed upon them, as
written above, "forasmuch as they refused the waters of Shiloah" (Isa. 8:6). Their sins did this: that the Lord set up over them a shepherd who
"feeds himself" (Ezek. 34:2), and "the flock he did not feed" (cf. Ezek. 34:3) with knowledge and understanding, but only with mockery of the words
of Torah and scorn of those who study it. From then on lawlessness prevailed, for our many sins: "without, the sword shall bereave" (Deut. 32:25).
And the said great and powerful leader, R. B[er] K[ohen], was very pleased with such a rabbi, for he obeyed him in everything; for R. Y[eḥezkel]
understood and knew between the lashes of R. B[er] K[ohen]'s eyes, and called him "zeide", that is, my grandfather — for so they call a
grandfather in the Polish language: zeide. And when they asked him something in the affairs of the community or of individuals, he would first
investigate and inquire and ask: "What does zeide say in this matter?" And according to what he was told, he did the mind, desire and will of R.
B[er] K[ohen], and paid no attention at all to others, whether it went well or ill with them — it did not matter to him — so long as his deeds were
right in the eyes of the said rich old man, the man of violence. In this he was careful with all his ability, so as to find favour in his eyes and
in the eyes of his sons, his sons-in-law, his friends and his acquaintances, who were all at the height of standing


והחשיבות באותו זמן, על כן היה ירא מהם מאד, גם הראה להם חבה יתירה, לאשר היתה הנאתו קרובה מהם במדה מרובה לפי עשירותו הגדולה של רב"ך ובניו ואוהביו, ועם זה לא הפסיד כלום אצל עשירים אחרים, אדרבה כל שכן שהיו מוסיפים לו ולבניו מתנותיהם ודורונותיהם גם הם, למען ימצאו חן בעיניו כשיצטרכו אליו, כי הרב בג"ק הי"ל ממשלה גדולה על היחידים הן בעסקי הקהל והתמניות ומשפטים ודיני ממונות, הכל בידו בכח מוחלט, והיו מפחדים ממנו מאד, כי יוכל לפסוק חיותם ממש, וכאשר כה עשה לכמה בני אדם מחשובי הקהלה, ובסבתו ירדו מנכסיהם הורידום עד עפר, ע"י עינוי ועיוות הדין שעשה להם. ביחוד גרם רעה רבה למשפחות גדולות יקרות וחשובות שבכל הג"ק, ה"ה משפחת ר' משה ר' ליבש, הק' התורני המופלג הנ"ל, ומשפחת מחו' הק' הגדול ר"מ ר' נתן שיסדו הקהלה באלטונא, והיו אנשים גדולים עשירים כבירים, חכמים לומדים ויראי שמים, ובסבתו נעקרו ונשרשו ר"ל; בזכרי זאת מעי מתחחכין. גם הדבר מגיע אלינו, שהפסדנו ע"י כך סך ממון מסוים כנ"ל; אך שתי המשפחות הנ"ל כלו בענים בעו"ה, והמעט שנשאר מהם כמתים חשובים ר"ל.
ואם לא היה פועל רי"ח במשך זמן רבנות שלו, רק זה הרע לבד ראוי לפרסמו, לקחת ממנו דוגמא לדורות, להתפלל להי"ת שיצילם ממנהג צבור כזה, רחמנא לצלן, רחמנא לשזבן, אבל באמת הרבה יותר מזה גרם רעה להג"ק, כמעט קעקע כל הבירה ומחה והפך אותן כקערה. מה אומר ואדבר ואספרה, כמה מהרעות שסבב רי"ח! הן אלה קצות דרכי בני ביתו וגדוליו, ומי יוכל לספר אפילו חלק אחד מהן. מעתה אין חידוש ולא תימה אם נעשה בבתי קצינים דברים בלתי הגונים, שהיה להם ממי ללמוד ולדון קל"ו [א], אין להאריך מזה. רק אחת היתה פרוצה שנשמעו עליה דברים מכוערים ע"פ עד אחד, ורצה רי"ח לכוף אותה להוציאה מבעלה, שלא כהלכה לגמרי לפי דעתי, אע"פ שלא רציתי לטפל בה כלל לא נזדקקתי לעין בדינה, רק ע"פ מה ששלח לידי רמ"ח ע"ה, שנטפל ג"כ עם רי"ח בדבר זה, להוציא אשה מבעלה בכפיה שלא כדין. מתוך אותן הדברים והגביות עדות שקבלו, לא מצאתי מה שיספיק לאסור האשה על בעלה, ולכוף על הגט חלילה, לא ירד בני עמהם, וכמו שהודעתי לרמ"ח דעתי עודני בעמדן, כששלח הדין אלי לעיין בו, וגם ככה אמרתי לדייני

and importance at that time. Therefore he was very afraid of them, and also showed them great affection, since his benefit from them was near and
in large measure, according to the great wealth of R. B[er] K[ohen], his sons and his friends. With this he lost nothing with other rich men; on
the contrary, all the more did they add gifts and presents to him and his sons, they too, so as to find favour in his eyes when they needed him.
For the rabbi in the Three Communities had great power over the householders, both in the affairs of the community and appointments and in judgments
and money cases — everything was in his hand with absolute power — and they were very afraid of him, for he could literally cut off their
livelihood. So he did to several people among the important men of the community, and because of him they came down from their property; they
brought them down to the dust, through the torment and perversion of justice he did them. Especially he caused great evil to great, precious and
important families in all the Three Communities: namely the family of R. Moses R. Leibush's, the outstanding learned leader mentioned above, and the
family of my relative(?), the great leader R. M. R. Nathan's, who founded the community in Altona. They were great men, mightily rich, wise,
learned and God-fearing; and because of him they were uprooted and torn out, God save us. When I remember this my bowels are troubled. The thing
touches us too, for through this we lost a certain sum of money, as said above. But the two said families were utterly ruined, for our many sins,
and the few who remain of them are counted as dead, God save us.

Even if R. Y[eḥezkel] had done nothing during the time of his rabbinate but this evil alone, it would be fitting to publish it, to take an example
from it for the generations, to pray to the Blessed One to save them from such leadership of the public — "may the Merciful save us, may the
Merciful deliver us." But in truth he caused the Three Communities far more evil than this; he almost razed the whole citadel, and wiped and turned
it "as one wipes a dish" (2 Kgs. 21:13) ⟨S: a caret, pointing to the first passage of the typed insert that follows⟩. What shall I say and speak and
tell — how many of the evils that R. Y[eḥezkel] brought about! ⟨S: a mark Y, pointing to the second passage of the typed insert that follows⟩ "Lo,
these are but the outskirts of the ways" (Job 26:14) of his household and his great ones; and who can tell even one part of them?

From now on it is no novelty and no wonder if improper things were done in the houses of leaders, who had someone to learn from and to argue a
fortiori [a]. There is no need to dwell on this ⟨S: a six-line note: "in any case nothing was heard of a prohibition of a married woman in all the
Three Communities, God forbid, but only the haughtiness of the feeling(?) that they had in their heart"⟩, except that one woman was loose, about whom
ugly things were heard on the testimony of one witness, and R. Y[eḥezkel] wanted to compel her to leave her husband — not according to the law at
all, in my opinion. Although I did not want to deal with it at all, and did not undertake to look into her case, but only according to what R. M.
Ḥ., peace be upon him, sent me — for he too was involved with R. Y[eḥezkel] in this matter, to take a woman from her husband by compulsion, not
according to the law — from those words and the collected testimony they had received, I did not find what would suffice to forbid the woman to her
husband and to compel a divorce, God forbid; "my son did not go down with them" (cf. Gen. 42:38). As I made known my opinion to R. M. Ḥ. while I was
still in Emden, when he sent the case to me to examine; and so too I said to the judges of

made false charges against her, and they excommunicated him in Altona. That man was an outstanding scholar, of the noble families of the land of
Poland, and feared the Lord more than many; that is why he did this and despised the wife of his youth with all her property and sent her away with
a bill of divorce, and he went out from there naked and in want of all things, wandering for bread.

Another, on her own word against(?) her husband [a] — namely the daughter of Gumprecht, wife of R. Z. Danzig, who had several children — once came

husband; and so this man did, and made the matter known"⟩; and afterwards he was forced to release her from the prohibition and annul his decree.

For all that, I covered up for him, and did not want to speak of his disgrace and provoke him for many years, for he too showed me great affection,
after he saw that I did him and his house no harm at all; on the contrary, he had relief through me. Therefore he [told] my praise before everyone,
and came to my house at every festival. I too left him his honour; I said, "there is old age here" (cf. b. Shabbat 152a), and he had attained
greatness. Although the sins [of the generation caused that the rabbis could not] agree on the law, I therefore fought for him with all my strength,
though he was not worthy; and he also showed that [R. S. Ḥ. and R. M. Ḥ.] were mistaken in the whole matter [c]. In any case, in the essence of the
matter his ruling was right this time; therefore I went out to the help of the truth and spent a great deal of my money on it, and had no benefit
from my labour and toil at all.

Again a case arose of a widow bound to a levir, and he included me too, and sent me his messenger with a responsum, to examine it at his urging and
request. I sent him my responsum too, in writing and with acceptance, and he and his court examined it and said with a full mouth [that my words were
right, and that there was no] witness and proof sufficient to permit her. That woman, called Ḥayyah, remained in the chains of the prohibition some
weeks. But the betrothed was of the relatives of her husband ⟨S: a note at the foot of the margin, continuing off the page: "the one standing(?) …"⟩,
and they preferred death to life for their kinsman, so that his name would be forgotten from Israel,

השכימו לפתחו של רי"ח יום יום ופתוהו ויכלו לו, ועל פי הנשמע ע"י הסרסור הגדול ]ר"ז התיר האשה[, ואת הכל פתאום לפתע עשו להזוקוקה [א], בלי הגיד לשום אדם, על מה דתא מהחצפא להשיא לשוק יבמה העומדת בחזקת איסור, אף כי אותי הצעיר לא קרא להיות נמנה להתיר; אחר שהייתי באותו מנין לאסור ונתקבלה דעתי, היה מהראוי עכ"פ לגלות אזני ולהודיעני טעמו של דבר. ובעת ההיא הייתי עסוק בהדפסת ספר שאילת יעב"ץ ועומד באותו ענין, כדומה לי שהיה כתוב אצלי מאז, וההעתק ממנו שלחתיו ג"כ לרי"ח עם תשובתי הנ"ל, על כן קבעתי גם נדון הלז אצלי תוך ספרי, ובי תולה אומן המסדר, ומדפיס שלי היה בחור ]אוהב[ לרי"ח, הוא גילה הדבר לרי"ח [ב] והלך וקבל עלי על זה לפו"מ, שהיו עושים כל רצונו באשר היה נוהג לישא פנים בכל עסקי הקהל עם יחידים, שאע"פ שהיה לו כח ויכולת גדול ועצום מן המיר"ה, וכפי תקנת הקהלות בלעדו לא ירים איש ידו, לדון שום יחיד, הוא היה מניח אנשי הקהל כל חפצם, להכביד עולם על היחידים כרצונם, ולהטיל עליהם אימה יתירה, כפי הישר בעיניהם ונטיות דעת המופשט בלבד, ועל זה גדלה הצעקה הרבה מאד, ואין מושיע כמש"ל, לפיכך נמצאו לו מיד לכל בקשתו מהם, ולא דקדקו אחריו והשליכו אשמם בראשם, ועשו מעשה תיכף ומיד להעביר כרוז בבה"כ הגדולה, על המדפים שלי אהרן זעציר, ואסרו הדפוס שלו, וזה עני היתה פרנסתו מצויה לו על ידי בעזה"י, שהייתי משלם לו שכר פעולתו, בעין יפה וגומל חסד עמו, לא בלבד להקדים לו שכרו, אבל גם הלויתי לו סך מסוים בחנם, ואף בלי משכון או בלתי ]שט"ח[, וע"י המאורע הלז קפחו פרנסתו של העני הלז, גם הלואתו שהאמנתיו לערך מאה ר"ט נאבד, ונשאר מלות חן וחסד אצלו, והיה צועק ואינו נענה; ורי"ח אוטם אזנו מזעקת הדל, אף אנכי צווחתי ככרוכיא ולית דעני; והלכתי לוועד הקהל וספר אגרת בקורת בידי, והיו נאספים כל פו"מ ורי"ח עמהם יושב אצלם בפעם ההיא, והצעתי דברי טענותי לפניהם, ותלונתי הכפולה על החמס שעושים לעני, שחייו תלויים בי בעת ההיא, והעושק שגורמים לי במעשה הזר, שעשו בלי דרישה וחקירה רק ע"פ בקשת רי"ח, ואמרתי להם שמעו נא מילי:

rose early to R. Y. Ḥ.'s door day after day, enticed him and prevailed over him (cf. Judg. 16:5). And on the word heard
through the great broker [R. Z. permitted the woman], they suddenly did the whole thing at once for the bound woman
[a], without telling anyone — by what law? out of impudence — to marry off "abroad" (Deut. 25:5) a levirate widow who
stood under a presumption of prohibition. Me, the young one, he did not even call to be counted among those who permit;
yet since I had been in that quorum to forbid, and my opinion had been accepted, he ought at least to have uncovered my
ear and let me know the reason of the thing. At that time I was busy printing the book She'ilat Ya'avetz, and was just
at that subject; as it seems to me, it had been written down with me since then, and I had also sent the copy of it to
R. Y. Ḥ. with my responsum mentioned above. So I set this case too in my book. And since (?) the craftsman who set
the type, my printer, was a young man [devoted] to R. Y. Ḥ., he revealed the matter to R. Y. Ḥ. [b], who went and
complained of me over it to the parnassim and leaders. They did all his will, as he was accustomed to show favour in all
the affairs of the community with private persons: for although he had great and mighty power and ability from His
Majesty, and by the ordinance of the communities "without him no man shall lift up his hand" (Gen. 41:44) to judge any
private person, he let the men of the community have all their desire, to lay a heavy yoke on private persons as they
pleased and to cast excessive dread on them, as was right in their eyes and by the bent of their bare opinion alone.
Over this the outcry grew very great, and there was no one to save, as I wrote above. Therefore they were at once ready
for him in all he asked of them; they did not look closely into it, and they cast the guilt on their own heads. They
acted forthwith to have a proclamation passed in the Great Synagogue against my printer, Aaron Setzer, and forbade his
press. This poor man had his livelihood through me, with God's help, for I paid him the wage of his work generously and
did him kindness: not only did I pay his wage in advance, but I also lent him a certain sum free, without even a pledge
or a [bond]. Through this event they cut off this poor man's livelihood; his loan too, about a hundred Reichstaler, which
I had trusted him with, was lost, and remained with him as a loan of favour and kindness. He cried out and was not
answered; R. Y. Ḥ. "stopped his ear at the cry of the poor" (Prov. 21:13). I too "cried out like a crane, and no one
answered". I went to the council of the community with the book Iggeret Bikoret in my hand. All the parnassim and
leaders were gathered, and R. Y. Ḥ. sat with them at that time. I set out my claims before them, and my double complaint
over the violence they were doing to the poor man, whose life hung on me at that time, and the wrong they were doing me by
this strange deed, which they did without inquiry and investigation, only at R. Y. Ḥ.'s request. I said to them, "Hear now my
words" (cf. Job 34:2): Behold, your head of the court sits here opposite me; let trustworthy men tell [whether] it was

לבי גם בהוראה מימי היותי כאן, והגידו נא אם ]אתערב[ בעסקי צבור או יחידים מרצוני, רק כאשר אני נתבע ונשאל מאתכם או מאב"ד שלכם, על כרחי ונגד רצוני נקראתי לפעמים לעיין בדין והוראה, כי היכא דלמטייא שיבא מכשורא, ולא יכולתי לסרב לזקן ולכבודכם; my heart, also in giving rulings, since the days I have been here. Tell now whether I [meddled] ⟨S: "I
involved myself"⟩ in the affairs of the congregation or of private persons of my own will. Only when I was summoned and asked
by you or by your head of the court was I sometimes called, against my will and against my wish, to look into a case of
law and ruling — for where the chip of the beam strikes [one, one cannot escape] — and I could not refuse the old man and
your honours. Once I strove his strife and fought for him with all my strength, when he took counsel with me; I also
wrote long responsa to rescue him from the hand of his critics, and also raised them on the altar of the press "for
acceptance before the Lord" (Lev. 1:3), to defend the Torah of truth with all might; and I spent my own money on it, from
my own pocket alone, without any help or benefit in the world, as you see in this book, Iggeret Bikoret, which I have
set before you. Then my words were good, right, pleasing and accepted by your head of the court. And now in this case,
when they compelled [me] once more to look into his ruling — though the matter was hard in my eyes, for [I am] one of
those who fear to give rulings — I could not escape doing his desire, and did his will. This time I could not agree with
him, for there is no favouring in the Torah; and so the court [heard] my words and admitted with full mouth that that
woman may not be permitted. And now suddenly a deed is done, without notice given first [to a man] like me, this
day. Although "I am young in years and he is very old" (Job 32:6), nevertheless, since at his request I undertook to
look into the matter and write on it, justice requires [that] he should not do so great a deed without uncovering my ear
and letting me know his reason for going back on the first agreement and changing his will within a single hour —
especially as it is a matter of forbidden unions, and we all sit in one ship, and no one may bore a hole beneath himself
in the place where he sits, and all Israel are sureties for one another; all the more the one who was asked and joined to
the matter: the duty lies on him. Those who own the beam must go into the thickness of the beam, as one agrees (?) who
pursues his soul's mischief (?). At any rate I want to know the reason for the permission now; though I kept myself out
of it at first, and never said, Accept my opinion; rather I say, I am your disciple and will drink your water. "If the
waters are sure" (Isa. 33:16), it will not be to me "as a deceitful brook" (Jer. 15:18). Now, so that your words may be
justified, "and I will not remove the speech of the trusty" (Job 12:20). But he was like a mute who did not open his
mouth to answer, "either good or bad" (Gen. 31:24); only the parnassim and leaders spoke for him and said to me: He need
not give a reason or a proof; what he has done is done and cannot be undone. And I said: Not so; he is bound and obliged,
not only to clear himself of suspicion and to show that he is "guiltless before the Lord and before Israel" (Num. 32:3),
but it is Torah and we must learn, to fix the law; and "he who withholds corn" (Prov. 11:26) shall not be free of
punishment. With all the reasons I multiplied in my words, to tip him to the side of merit so that he would explain his
ruling, I gained nothing: as one speaking to the trees and the stones. But the parnassim and leaders said: So we
understand and decree, that I shall not meddle in this matter and shall not publish it in print at all. Then I answered
them: I do not want your decree, harder than Pharaoh's, who did not decree to annul the Torah and break the law; and since

come at me in roundabout ways, and I speak words of reason and have no one to hear me, and none of you answers his words
with knowledge and understanding, while he wants to be thought a wise man who keeps silent — therefore I may not keep
silent, and I pay no heed to your decree, for it is of your own making; the judgement of the Torah is not handed over to
you. I will write, if need be (?), to the great men of our time, and seek the word of the Lord, and we shall see whose
word will stand (cf. Jer. 44:28); "at their mouth shall the matter be established" (Deut. 19:15) — not as you say and
decree without reason [a]. With this I took leave of you in anger and wrath.

Afterwards they sent their messenger, the cantor, to me again, with the word in his mouth that I should take care and
beware not to print this affair, and not to publish it in a book all the days of R. Y. Ḥ.'s life. In my place I stood
ready to answer them boldly that I would do as my Maker directs me. Nevertheless I ruled my spirit and kept their decree,
for I said: I am not obliged to give my life for this; it is enough for me that "I have delivered my soul" (Ezek. 3:19),
and the Lord will repay the evildoer according to his evil, and the chain hangs on whoever can protest, not
on me, for these men are too hard for me (2 Sam. 3:39). So I did not write to anyone outside. But I heard that the rabbi
R. A. of Brody, of blessed memory, who was head of the court in Amsterdam at that time — R. Y. Ḥ. had consulted him too
and asked his opinion, and he did not agree to permit but only to forbid. When he heard of the marriage of the bound
woman, he was very angry, and "bowed down so that he could not hear" (Isa. 21:3).

Before I went out of the seat of the council of the parnassim and leaders, to which I had come to complain of their
decree, I spoke harshly to R. Z. F. here, who was R. Y. Ḥ.'s advocate and gave him strong support, and I said these words
to him: Hear now, R. Z.: I know that you do not say this from your own heart, nor do you support R. Y. Ḥ. against the
law of the Torah; you are afraid of Popper (for the man ⟨S: "the apostate"⟩ was his uncle, and R. Z. was bent under R.
Y. P., as his end proved); for this reason ⟨S: "but for"⟩ you would not have done this to me. For our many sins, not many
weeks passed before (pursued) [R. Z. F.] was ruined in a great bankruptcy and remained Popper's debtor; at R. Y. P.'s
suit they sentenced R. Z., peace be upon him, and his mind was deranged, God save us, in an evil way. Then also began to
be fulfilled what my father, of blessed memory, said about the house of R. B. K. From then on all the descendants of R.
B. K. went down lower and lower, to "a loaf of bread" (1 Sam. 2:36), God save us.

שלא כהוגן, שהיתה יבמה זקוקה גמורה, ולכן מן השמים הפרישום מן האיסור. ]אחר איזה[ שנים נפטרו גם שניהם בלי שילדה לו, אע"פ שהיתה האשה ילדה בשנים, והי"ל בנים מבעלה הראשון אבל מתו בחייו, גם בעלה השני שנשאה באיסור, הי"ל בנים מאשתו הראשונה, גם מאשה שנשא אחריה, אע"פ שרי"ח הכחיש הידוע כמ"ש ]בספרי הנ"ל[.
עוד קרה פ"א בפני, שאשה אחת באה אליו ואמרה שנטמאת תחת אישה, שהיה ב"ב נכבד מקק"א היה נקרא ר"ז, והיה בדנציג בעת ההיא, ולו כמה בנים ממנה והיתה מרגלת קטטה עמו, על שעזבה זמן מה ופירש ממנה, ונסע לארץ אחרת, לפי שהיתה מפזרת בלתי הסתפקות, ולא חסה על ממונו וביתו אינה שומרת, ועל כן שנאה והניחה והלך לו, והיא יושבת בדוחק עם בניה, כנראה להנקם ממנו עשתה זאת, והאשה ההיא ג"כ בת איש אחד מסוים, ב' גומפריכט שהיה קצין גדול לפנים, ובעת ההיא כבר ירד מנכסיו, ע"כ לא עשה רי"ח עוד חשבון ממנו, בדרכו לישא פנים לעשירי קהלתו אפילו במקום שאין משא פנים כנ"ל, והכריז עליה שהיא פרוצה זונה, ואביה הנ"ל בא אלי וסיפר לי בקובלנא רבה על הנעשה לבתו באין מוחים, ואמרתי שאם כך הדברים, אזי ודאי לא יפה עשה רי"ח, ואינו רשאי לשתוק ולסבול, כי אין הדבר נוגע לכבוד בלבד, אבל הוא שלא כהלכה, לפי שאין האשה נאמנת לאסור עצמה על בעלה, ויכול לגרום להרבות ממזרים בישראל, אם יכוף את הבעל לתת גט מעושה שלא כדין, גם יש בו משום הוצאות לעז על הבנים, מלבד פגמה ופגם משפחה, לא יעשה כן בישראל; לפיכך יעצתיו שילך אל פו"מ ויספר להם כל העשוי לבתו שלא כתורה, וכן עשה והועילה עצתי ב"ה, כי אנשי הקהל גזרו עליו שיוציא האשה מן האיסור ומן הג"ד שפסק עליה, והכריחוהו לחזור ולעשות כרוז אחר לפרסם שהיא טהורה.
כי בימים ההם פו"מ מושלים על האב"ד הזקן ההוא, עם שהיתה ידו תקיפה על העניים ומרודים, כי לו היה כח ורשות מן המיר"ה, לדון ולהורות לקנוס ולענוש ולית דימחי בידו, ובודאי הי"ל ממשלה על הפו"מ, הם היו צריכין להיות כפופים ומוכניים תחתיו, אלא שהוא הכניע עצמו התחתיהם, ברצונו סר למשמעתם ועשה מצותם וגזרתם, ובזה מצא חן בעיני תקיפי הצבור ומשבחים אותו בענוה; אבל אוי לענוה פסולה כזאת שאינה אלא חנופה, להחזיק ביד העשירים וגברי תקיפי, לשעבד ביחידים כרצונם להנאתו הקרובה, ותועלתו הטובה מצויה לו עמהם בשלוה ואהבה, כי בזה האופן היו כגומלים זא"ז, הוא

unlawfully, for she was a widow fully bound to her levir; and so Heaven kept them apart from the forbidden thing. [After
some] years both of them died without her having borne him [a child], although the woman was young in years and had had
children by her first husband, who died in his lifetime; and her second husband, who married her in a forbidden way, had
children by his first wife and also by a wife he married after her — although R. Y. Ḥ. denied what was known, as I
wrote [in my book mentioned above].

Another thing happened once in my presence. A woman came to him and said that she had been defiled while under her
husband. He was a respected householder of the holy community of Altona, called R. Z., and he was in Danzig at that time.
He had several children by her, and she used to stir up quarrels with him, because he had left her for some time,
separated from her and travelled to another country; for she was wasteful beyond measure, did not spare his money and
did not keep his house. So he hated her, left her and went away, and she lived in straits with her children. It seems she
did this to take revenge on him. That woman was also the daughter of a distinguished man, B. Gumprecht, who had been a
great leader in former times and by then had already lost his property. Therefore R. Y. Ḥ. took no more account of him —
in his way of favouring the rich men of his community, even where there is no room for favour, as said above — and he
proclaimed her a harlot and a whore. Her father came to me and told me, with a great complaint, what had been done to his
daughter with no one protesting. I said that if things were so, then certainly R. Y. Ḥ. had not done well, and he must
not keep silent and bear it; for the matter does not touch honour alone, but it is against the law, since a woman is not
believed when she forbids herself to her husband. It may lead to multiplying bastards in Israel, if he compels the husband
to give a forced divorce unlawfully; it also brings slander on the children, besides her own blemish and the blemish of
the family: "no such thing ought to be done in Israel" (2 Sam. 13:12). So I advised him to go to the parnassim and leaders
and tell them all that had been done to his daughter against the Torah. He did so, and my advice helped, thank God: the
men of the community decreed that he must release the woman from the prohibition and from the sentence he had passed on
her, and they compelled him to go back and make another proclamation, publishing that she was pure.

For in those days the parnassim and leaders ruled over that old head of the court, though his hand was strong over the
poor and the afflicted; for he had power and authority from His Majesty to judge and to rule, to fine and to punish, and
no one could stay his hand. Surely he should have had dominion over the parnassim and leaders; they should have been bent
and subject under him. But he humbled himself beneath them; of his own will he turned to their obedience and did their
commands and decrees. By this he found favour in the eyes of the strong men of the congregation, and they praised him for
humility. But woe to such a faulty humility, which is nothing but flattery: to strengthen the hand of the rich and the
strong men, to subject private persons to their will, for his own near benefit; his good profit came to him from them in
peace and love, for in this way they repaid one another. He

strengthened their hands in every wrong they did to private persons. Those who had no hand with them and were not in
their favour, and those who were not dear to him — and they too supported his hands — when he perverted the way for them,
they "cried out violence and were not answered" (cf. Job 19:7): "between the midwife and the woman in labour," etc.
[a]. To people from whom he had no benefit he was not humble, but hard as stone. In this alone he behaved like a
scholar: "taking revenge and bearing a grudge like a serpent" (b. Yoma 23a). Whoever he had some grudge against in his
heart, he lay in wait for him and did not rest until he had taken his revenge on him. As for the perversions of justice he
committed, "the bed is too short to stretch oneself" (Isa. 28:20), for a large book would not hold them. Before midday he
would rule one way, and after midday "another spirit was with him" (Num. 14:24). And so he and his court were suspected of
bribery in particular, and there were many grounds for the thing. A man held to be trustworthy told me that he had a case
before his court, and one of the judges asked what his reward would be if he decided the case in his favour; and there was
an unceasing rumour that they demanded their share with their own mouths. Woe to the ears that hear such things, woe to
the generation in whose days such a thing came about! From estates he took whatever his heart desired, things beyond
measure. I heard that from the estate of Solomon Yaff' he took, of plain silverware, a weight of eight hundred loth for his
share, and many more like this. From there he grew rich, and gave lavish dowries to his daughters. But "as it came, so it
went" (cf. Eccl. 5:15) to perdition: for the daughters he married off died in his lifetime, some years after their
weddings, and he lost his daughters together with the great wealth he had given them; much of what he had robbed also went
to perdition, and that wealth was lost "in an evil venture" (Eccl. 5:13), through the evil breeding there was in his house,
as said above, besides what is not mentioned here.

But this community grew poor in his days, for our many sins, through the sin of robbery and false oaths, which multiplied
in his time, for they were a joke in their eyes and counted as permitted. Therefore in the end he lost the Jewish
jurisdiction over Hamburg, where his hand had been strong at first, as in Altona; for so the Three Communities had been
founded: they had one judgement in civil cases, by their rabbi, the head of the court. But the councillors of that great
city mentioned were weary of hearing the people's outcry against R. Y. Ḥ., their rabbi, in judgements and rulings; so they
took this power from them and decreed that no one from the community of Hamburg should go before the head of the court of
the Three Communities, to this day (and from ⟨S: "the abomination"⟩ Eybeschütz ⟨S: "may the name of the wicked rot"⟩ the
power was taken away in Altona too, as I wrote above with God's help: "and it came to pass in the days when the judges
judged" (Ruth 1:1), "who turn aside to their crooked ways" (Ps. 125:5)).

And what shall we say of his teaching, his novellae, his plain interpretations and his sermons? They were truly "jest and
mockery"; it would not be believed if all the madness were told, and the idle words, fancies, "vexation of spirit and
vanities" (Eccl. 1:14), so that all who heard them filled their mouths with laughter in spite of themselves. And at his
rulings and decisions every man of knowledge and understanding would be astonished, as they are written down with me; and
these are only a little part

of much. His book too, which he brought to print as a witness — I have set a little of it as a mere sample in the book
She'ilat Ya'avetz. Trustworthy men told me that in the holy community of F[rankfurt] too, the head of the court, our
teacher R. Y. Katz, of blessed memory, and other scholars said that the book Keneset Yeḥezkel [a] ought to be
burned. Of his errors and mistakes in simple things I will also mention only a very little, as a sign.

In Altona it happened once that when the cantor R. Y., peace be upon him, read from the Torah in the synagogue before the
congregation "and you shall look upon the birthstool" (Ex. 1:16) with kamatz under the alef, R. Y. Ḥ. rebuked the
cantor and said to him: You are wrong, for one must say ha-avanim with kamatz under the bet, meaning stones (because
of what Rashi explained [?]). So expert was he in reading the written [Torah]; and so did he know the oral [Torah], in the
Talmud. Once he taught the Gemara of Megillah and came to the passage: "What did Esther see that she invited Haman? R.
Eliezer says: She hid traps (paḥim) for him" [b]. He thought it was like pakhim, jugs, as in "a jug in a spoon",
and explained the word: she hid jugs for him, Krüglich in German. And in Rosh ha-Shanah: "All who come into the world
pass before Him like benei maron, and all of them are surveyed in one survey (sekirah)" [c]: he explained that
they are marked with red paint (sikra), as one marks the tithe. And many such things were with him; whoever hears will
laugh [at him, and there is no] need to lengthen on this. Far be it from me to mention anything but what is very well known
and cannot be denied; and at this time there are still several people who know of these things and the like.

When he first sat on the rabbinic throne of the Three Communities, the pious man, eminent in Torah, R. G. Schnapper, of
blessed memory, said of him: If R. Y. Ḥ. had come before me, when I was treasurer of the Talmud Torah, for permission to be
a children's teacher in the Three Communities, I would not have given it to him. With all this he ruled with great pride
and with violence beyond measure; and even so he got himself a name as a humble and patient man, also through the sins of
the generation. In truth his eye was evil; he did all his heart desired, and sat and made sport of the people who were
pressed by him. They were angry at him and at his evil affairs, and sometimes, out of their pain, they flung hard words
against him from the great bitterness of their hearts; and he heard and kept silent, and answered them with much mockery:
Go to the Blessed Name and summon me to judgement! This was his humility. Yet he had in his hand stick and strap, to rule
the people by force, with no one able to protest against him. In this he was clever: he did not rouse his anger, but
suppressed his wrath, only doing all his will with laughter; and at his ease he took revenge on his enemies, knowing they
were sure to fall into his hand. So he had no need to pain his heart in any way. He loved himself, guarded his strength and
his health, and "made his heart merry" (cf. Judg. 19:6) with constant drink: he always had wine and mead and fine, spiced
wine in plenty. For this he had

a special place in his house, with vessels and workmen to prepare these drinks in particular, of the choicest
possible (?), such as no leader in the world had; besides his food, delicacies of the world, which were found in his house
like dust. [He lacked nothing] to disturb his rest; so he saw no reason to trouble his joy and his pleasures through anger
and vexation. Nevertheless he saw [his desire] on his enemies, for fortune smiled on him. He paid no heed to the poor of
the people and did not turn his heart to their cry; for R. B. K. had obtained for him the licence of His Majesty, which
gave him great power to rule over the poor people by force, even to throw men into prison and to keep them desolate in
confinement on his word and decree alone. No one was allowed to question him; the officers of the law of the gentiles and
their bailiffs did his command and kept his orders, by the licence of His Majesty. And all the time that R. B. K. was
alive, R. Y. Ḥ. did his will, as said above; and they used to say of this: The Greek dances the dance of [the bear], Bär
in the German language [a].

He had another quality, good for himself: whenever he said something foolish and silly and saw people laughing at his
words, he was [glad] and of good heart, for he thought that it came from their great joy and delight in the pleasure of the
novel interpretations they had heard from his mouth, which were sweet to them and "sweeter than honey" (Ps. 19:11), and
that they delighted greatly; [and therefore] they had gladness and joy. In truth they despised him and mocked him, and he
was in their eyes like one who jests, a laughing-stock. Yet he was not so foolish as to grieve himself, so as not to harm
[his body]; he made himself as if he did not know that they laughed at his dreams and his words, and he went out "glad and
of a good heart" (Esth. 5:9), and said with full mouth that he had won a good name by his sermon, and boasted [of it
greatly].

Added to his many delights was constant drinking, of wine and raisin brandy (?) and other drinks, always in a row; he ate
and drank all his days. And since he had a strong nature and was coarse, hard as stone, his life was sweet, pleasant and
good; for all he did, learned and wrought in the world was good and lovely in his eyes. He never saw any fault in himself,
and his heart was glad in his own folly and in every ugly deed. Only when he obtained silver and gold was his heart full
of joy, and he thought there was none like him; for the star of his luck helped him in all his ways, a thing to wonder at
(only in the last eighteen [years] he saw evils, and in some of them he also saw joys). He prospered in his deeds all
the days of his life, even when they were most ugly; but the community went down lower and lower to the bottom of the pit,
and with all this his heart was sound and stout (Ps. 73:4). He could sit day and night drinking and getting drunk, for he
made his feast much in every place and with everyone, especially at a feast of circumcision or a wedding, in the company of
the ignorant and the light-minded, until he was a laughing-stock in the eyes of the mass of the people

בכלל. והנכבדים היו מתכיישים על שהיה מזלזל כל כך ומחלל כבוד התורה בפומבי, לכן הוצרכו פו"מ לגזור עליו שלא ילך לכל סעודה אם לא אצל הגדולים ובמקום שנתנו לו חלק במצוה לא זולת. עוד היה זקן כמותו עוסק בדברים בטלים הרבה, ותמיד הי"ל בביתו ישיבת ע"ה ויושבי קרנות שמודיעים לו כל החדושים המתהוים בעולם ובקהלם ומקבלי לגימה ממנו. ביחוד היו לו תיורים וחוקרים מעמד ומצב כל יחיד ויחיד שבג"ק; ע"י כך היה בקי בהם ובמעשיהם, ויודע סתרי כולם אשר יעשו בחדרי משכיתם, מי עשיר ומי עני, מי הצריך להקפה ומי שכוכב מערכתו הולך ואור יפה או שוקע ורפה, ומי שיצטרך באיזה דבר משפט או זולת, לזווג זווגים לעסוק בשדוכים, ובכל אופן שיוכל להרבות הונו וממונו ואונו, וגם עי"ז היה יכול להנקם ג"כ מהאנשים אשר ידע שאינם מאוהביו, כי גלו אליו מסתורי כל איש ואיש, ודי הוה צבא הוה מרים, די הוה צבא הוה משפיל ובמי שהיה נותן עיניו, שלפי דעתו לא יצא י"ח נגדו במתנת פורים ור"ה כפי הערך אשר העריך אותו, היה לוקח נקמתו ממנו, בדבר משפט כשבא לפניו לדין, או בשומת ערך הקהל בעניני כבוד, או בעסקי מינוי פרנסים מנהיגים שופטים ושוטרים גבאים ודיינים, או להרע לו בענין שידוך, או להוציא עליו קול שאינו בעל כיס, למעט נאמנותו ולקפח פרנסתו; והיתה בידו רשימה בפורים ור"ה, שעוברין לפניו כבני מרון כל אנשי ג"ק, לראות ולעיין אם נפקד איש מהרגילים לשלוח אליו מתנותיהם בפרקים הללו בפרטות, ולדעת מי מהם המוסיף ומי הפוחת וגורע, או עוזב ומונע, ולפי הרשימה יהיה כל ריב ונגע, אשר תהיה ליחידי הקהלות הצריכים אליו, בדבר דין ומשפט בין איש ובין רעהו. וסיפר לי איש מסוים ות"ח, כי היה בק"א נכבד אחד שלא היה אוהבו, ולא היה רגיל לשלוח לו דורון; פעם אחד תבע האיש ההוא אדם אחד לעמוד עמו לדין לפני רי"ח, על שהיה חייב לו סך רב כמה מאות ר"ט, ולא היה יכול להוציאו, ועשה לו רי"ח כל טצדקי בעינוי ועות הדין, בתחבולות כל מה שיוכל, כדי לפטור את הנתבע עד שהפסיד זה מעותיו, שסבב לו כדי להנקם ממנו, על שמונע עצמו לפקדו במתנותיו; וכשראה והבין אותו ב"ב כך, והיו לו ב"ח רבים שהיה עוסק עמהם ונותן להם סחורות בהקפה ובאשראי, היה נמלך בעצמו ואומר על מה זה אגרום רעה לעצמי, להפסיד הרבה בשביל דבר מועט שאתן לו בפורים ור"ה, אם יהיה ר"ט ד"מ או פחות או יותר, זה איננו שוה בנזק שלי, להרויח אהבת הרב שיהא לי מעיר

at large. The notables were ashamed that he so cheapened and profaned the honour of the Torah in public; so the parnassim
and leaders had to decree that he should not go to every feast, but only to the great men's, and to a place where they gave
him a share in the commandment, and nowhere else. Moreover, old man as he was, he busied himself much with idle things, and
he always had in his house a sitting of ignorant men and "those who sit in the corners" (b. Avodah Zarah 18b), who told him
all the news that happened in the world and in their community, and took a mouthful from him. Above all he had spies and
investigators of the standing and state of every single person in the Three Communities; through this he knew them and
their deeds, and knew the secrets of all of them, what they did "in their chambers of imagery" (Ezek. 8:12): who was rich
and who poor, who needed credit, and whose star was rising and shining or sinking and weak, and who would need some lawsuit
or the like, to make matches and deal in marriage brokerage, and in every way by which he could increase his wealth, his
money and his power. Through this he could also take revenge on the people he knew were not among his friends, for the
secrets of every man were revealed to him: "whom he would he raised up, and whom he would he put down" (Dan. 5:19). And on
whoever he set his eyes, who in his opinion had not done his duty toward him in the Purim gift and the New Year gift
according to the assessment he had made of him, he took his revenge: in a lawsuit when he came before him for judgement, or
in the community's assessment in matters of honour, or in the appointment of parnassim, leaders, judges and officers,
treasurers and judges, or to harm him in a marriage match, or to spread a rumour about him that he had no money, so as to
lessen his credit and cut off his livelihood. He had in his hand a list at Purim and the New Year, when all the men of the
Three Communities pass before him "like benei maron" (m. Rosh ha-Shanah 1:2), to see and examine whether anyone was
missing of those used to sending him their gifts at these seasons in particular, and to know which of them added and which
lessened and subtracted, or left off and withheld; and by the list was every dispute and every plague (Deut. 21:5) that the
private persons of the communities who needed him had, in a matter of law and judgement between a man and his fellow.

A distinguished man and scholar told me that there was in the holy community of Altona a respected man who did not love him
and was not used to sending him a gift. Once that man summoned a certain person to stand trial with him before R. Y. Ḥ.,
because he owed him a large sum, several hundred Reichstaler, and he could not get it out of him. R. Y. Ḥ. used every device
of delay and perversion of justice, with every trick he could, to acquit the defendant, until this man lost his money; he
brought this about to take revenge on him for withholding himself from remembering him with gifts. When that householder
saw and understood this, having many debtors with whom he dealt and to whom he gave goods on credit and on trust, he took
counsel with himself and said: Why should I bring harm on myself, to lose much for the sake of a small thing that I would
give him at Purim and the New Year? Whether it be four Reichstaler or less or more, it is not worth my damage, to gain the
love of the rabbi, who will rouse himself for me


לעזור לי בעת צרכי אליו, בעסק דין ודברים עם ב"ח שלי; וכן עשה. מהיום ההוא והלאה נהפך לאיש אחר, ונעשה אוהב ובמשפטו הרויח. באופן זה היה כופה האב"ד דג"ק הנ"ל את הב"ב שתחתיו לסור למשמעתו, ולהרבות לו מוהר ומתן (אוי לאזנים ששמעו כאלה קשות מהיושב על כסא המשפט והוראה. ונוכל לצייר מה הע"ה חושבים בלבם על תופסי התורה, ורבים מהם מוציאים מפיהם תר"ו [א], ומלעיבים במלאכי האלהים, כאילו כל הת"ח חשודים על הבצע) והיו יראים מפניו מאד, כי היה מכה בסתר ומטיל אימתו על הצבור ביותר, עם שהיה נקלה בעיניהם ובלבם כפי מעשיו הנ"ל, אבל לא הי"ל אפילו אוהב אחד בלב, חוץ מאיזה תקיפי הקהל שהיו מראים לו חבה לפנים, מחמת שהיה נושא פניהם ועושה כל חפצם, בהנקמם מאיש איש והכבדת עולם על היחידים, כי בזה היה עוזרם וסומך ידם, נמצא להם בכל עת ומבלעדו לא יכלו להוציא אל הפועל תאותם; כי כן נתיסדו תקנות הקהלות, שהרב אב"ד ידו תקיפה על פו"מ, בכל דבר אשר יסכימו עליו אין לו תוקף אם לא נעשה בחבר עיר, אבל הוא התיר ידם ועזב להם כל הממשלה, בין ביושר בין בעולה, (והיא שגרמה שנטל מהם הכבוד שרדפו אחריו בימיו, משלו בכח הזרוע ולא נכר דל לפני שוע, אח"כ ירדה פלאים מאיגרא רמה לבירא עמיקתא, מה שבידם נטל מהם לגמרי. בבוא אייבשיצר בא גם בוז, והיה כעם ככהן כמש"ל בס"ד, וזה הדבר שהיה עיקר הסבה להמחלוקת ופרוד לבבות, שכמעט משך אחריו חורבן הקהלות, לפי שמצאו היחידים עילה להנקם מפו"מ וליטול מהם הממשלה, כי אז חלק לבבם ותלו עצמן באיש הלז, למען יחזק ידיהם בהשפלת הפו"מ, ע"כ חזקו המה ידיו להגדילו ולהמשילו לגמרי, ועשה ככל אשר יזמו, להוריד כבוד הפו"מ עד עפר) וכן המה היו מסייעים אותו בעול שהיה עושה ליחידים לפעמים הדנים לפניו, ומחפים עליו מפני שהן כגומלין זא"ז.

to help me in time of need, in my lawsuits with my debtors. And so he did. From that day on he [the
rabbi] was turned into another man, became his friend, and he won his case.

In this way the head of the court of the Three Communities mentioned above compelled the householders under him to submit
to his authority and to "multiply dowry and gift" (Gen. 34:12) for him. (Woe to the ears that heard such hard things from
one who sits on the seat of judgement and ruling! We can picture what the ignorant think in their hearts of those who hold
the Torah; many of them utter with their mouths "may their spirit blow away" [a], and "mock the messengers of God"
(2 Chr. 36:16), as though all the scholars were suspected of greed.) They were very afraid of him, for he "smote in secret"
(Deut. 27:24) and cast his dread upon the congregation exceedingly, though he was despised in their eyes and in their
hearts according to his deeds mentioned above. He had not even one friend at heart, except some strong men of the community
who showed him affection outwardly, because he favoured them and did all they wished, in their taking revenge on this man
and that and laying a heavy yoke on private persons; for in this he helped them and supported their hands, and was at their
disposal at any time, and without him they could not carry out their desire. For so the ordinances of the communities were
established: that the rabbi, the head of the court, has strong authority over the parnassim and leaders; whatever they
agree on has no force unless it is done with the town's council (?). But he loosed their hands and left all the rule to
them, whether in uprightness or in wrong. (And this is what caused the honour they pursued in his days to be taken from
them: they ruled by the strength of the arm, "and the rich was not regarded more than the poor" (Job 34:19); afterwards
it fell wondrously "from a high roof to a deep pit" (b. Ḥagigah 5b), and what was in their hands was taken from them
altogether. When ⟨S: "the wicked"⟩ Eybeschütz came, "contempt came too" (Prov. 18:3), "and it was, as with the people, so
with the priest" (Isa. 24:2), as I wrote above with God's help. This was the chief cause of the strife and the division of
hearts, which almost drew after it the ruin of the communities; for the private persons found a pretext to take revenge on
the parnassim and leaders and to take the rule from them. Then their heart was divided, and they hung themselves on this
man, so that he would strengthen their hands in humbling the parnassim and leaders; therefore they strengthened his hands to
make him great and give him full rule, and he did all they devised, to bring the honour of the parnassim and leaders down
to the dust.) And so they [the parnassim] helped him in the wrong he sometimes did to the private persons who were judged
before him, and covered up for him, because they repaid one another.

He had this too for a portion, "a proverb and a byword" (Deut. 28:37): although he was faulty, "no speech had he, nor
voice" (cf. 1 Kgs. 18:26) except the voice of coins, and his songs and chirpings ⟨S: "his melodies(?) and chirpings"⟩
were strange, causing laughter and mockery to all who heard — even so he thought himself a great and wonderful cantor and
singer, and he prayed on festivals and the Days of Awe in the Great Synagogue, and went down before the ark to discharge
the duty of the many; and he caused jest and mockery

במקדש מעט, כל פעם שעמד בתפלה לפני העמוד. ומי שלא ראה או שמע מעשה נגוניו וקול צפצופיו, לא ראה שחוק מימיו, והיה ללעג ולקלס מרבה, עד שהלצנים המשחקים בבתי משתאות, כשהיו רוצים להרבות השחוק, ולהגדיל השמחה להיטיב לב העם הקרואים בבית המשתה, היו מתחילים לנגן ולשורר נגוניו של האב"ד הנ"ל עם כל תכונותיו ובתנועותיו להדמות אליו בעניניו, אז ימלא שחוק פי המסובים והנקבצים לשמחה, ותבקע הארץ לקולם, כי היו רגילים בכך ששון ושעשוע וטיול נפלא, עד שהיה מעורר להם השחוק בהפלגה גדולה, יותר ממה שצוחקים על מעשי הכסילים והשוטים הגמורים, או המתדמים ומצחקים ומשנים טעמם להתהולל כרקודין ומחולות. וכשבאה השמועה אליו לא הקפיד כלל, אדרבה גרמה לו שמחה עצומה ג"כ כמזכה הרבים, מאחר שממנו באה השמחה לרבים. וכבר היו שם בני אדם ושרים נמצאים לפעמים באותן מעמדות של שחוק, והיה קשה בעיניהם לשמוע השחוק וק"ר שעושין מן הרב אב"ד דג"ק, ולבם דוה מאד על זאת, כי היה ח"ה גדול וקלון לת"ח בפני ע"ה, ע"כ רצו למנוע אותן המשחקים בנגוניו בשכר על סעודות החתונות ובימי שמחה, והיו מוחין בידיהם וא"ל שלא יעשה ככה, ולא יתכן דבר זה מפני כבוד התורה וכבוד הצבור. אך מה עשה הוא, קרא אליו ביחוד נער אחד שהיה בקי לעשות אותן שריקות בפיו, ועשה דמיון נגוניו וצפצופיו בפני ההמון להרויח פרנסתו בזה, ואמר אל הנער בוא ואלמדך פרק שירה שלי, שמא אינך יודע עדיין להיטיב נגן כל הצורך, לכן שב בני ואמסור לך פרק בשיר שלי, שיהנו בו בני אדם מאד, ותוכל להרויח בזה ממון רב. כל כך גדלה הצלחת האיש הלז ברעיוניו, שאפילו מעשה שטות וכסילות היה גורם לו הנאה רבה מאד; ולא שהיה סכל כל כך, כי באמת בדבר תועלת עצמו בעניני ממון, היה פקח וערום גדול, אלא שכח המדמה שלו היה מטעה אותו, לרוב הצלחתו היה חושב מאין כמוהו בכל דבר מעלה ותהלה. גם שמשי הקהל והב"ד בימיו, כמושל מקשיב וגו', לוקחין מן היחידים בכל עת שיוכלו, כמוכס קצוב ושאינו קצוב. כשנשאתי אשתי שנייה ]נתתי כמה[ שוק [א], ונתתי בלי שום חקירה איך ומה, כי הייתי אז טרוד מאד, והזווג שלישי שנשאתי בת אחי, ולא ידעו אם יותן ]לי הרבה כסף[ לנדן, תבעו ממנו מלבד מה שבקש השמש לעצמו, ולא
[א] מין מטבע ובלע"ז Schock Heller.

in the "little sanctuary" (Ezek. 11:16), every time he stood in prayer before the reading desk. Whoever has not seen or
heard the performance of his melodies and the sound of his chirpings has never seen laughter in his life. He was a great
object of mockery and derision, so that the jesters who play in the drinking houses, when they wanted to increase the
laughter and enlarge the joy, to cheer the hearts of the people invited to the feast, would begin to play and sing the
melodies of the head of the court mentioned above, with all his manners and gestures, imitating him in his ways. Then the
mouths of the guests and of those gathered for the celebration were filled with laughter, "and the earth was rent with
the sound of them" (1 Kgs. 1:40); for they were used to this as a wonderful gladness, delight and amusement, until it
roused laughter in them far beyond the laughter at the deeds of fools and utter idiots, or of those who pretend, make sport
and change their behaviour to play the madman (1 Sam. 21:14) in dances and rounds. When the report reached him, he did not
mind at all; on the contrary, it gave him great joy too, as one who brings merit to the many, since joy came to the many
through him.

There were already men and officials present at times at such scenes of laughter, and it was hard in their eyes to hear the
laughter and scorn made of the rabbi, the head of the court of the Three Communities, and their hearts were very sick over
it, for it was a great profanation of the Name and a disgrace to scholars before the ignorant. So they wanted to stop those
players from [performing] his melodies for pay at wedding feasts and on days of rejoicing, and protested to them and told
them not to do so, for such a thing was not proper because of the honour of the Torah and the honour of the congregation.
But what did he do? He called to himself privately a boy who was skilled at making those whistlings with his mouth, and who
imitated his melodies and chirpings before the crowd to earn his living by it, and said to the boy: Come, and I will teach
you a chapter of my song, lest you do not yet know how to play it well enough; so sit, my son, and I will hand down to you a
chapter of my song, which people will enjoy very much, and you will be able to earn much money by it. So great was the
success of this man in his fancies, that even a deed of folly and stupidity brought him great pleasure. Not that he was such
a fool: in truth, in matters of his own benefit in money he was very shrewd and cunning; but his imagination misled him, and
from his great success he thought there was none like him in every matter of excellence and praise.

The beadles of the community and of the court in his days too — "if a ruler hearkens," etc. (Prov. 29:12) — took from
private persons at every time ⟨S: "pretext"⟩ they could, like a fixed and an unfixed tax-gatherer (cf. m. Bava Kamma
10:1). When I married my second wife, [I gave several] Schock [a], and I gave without any inquiry how and what, for I
was then very busy. And at the third match, when I married off my brother's daughter, and they did not know whether [much
money] would be given me for a dowry, they demanded from me ⟨S: a two-line note: "only (?) [for] the release of the
betrothal of the couple"⟩, besides what the beadle asked for himself, and not

רצה להעמיד החופה, עד שאתן תחלה מה שפסק עלי ]הקהל [א][ והוא ]האב"ד רי"ח[ ולא אאריך עוד במעשיו [ב].
בהיותי בהמבורג לפני איזה שבועות, הענין מה שכבר זכרתי למעלה, שהקצין כ' יואל שוא, אשר היה אוהב נאמן לאמ"ה ז"ל, נהפך לשונא אלי בסבתי שלקחתי אכסניא שלי בבית רב"ך מפני ההכרח כנ"ל, ואלה השנים היו שונאים זא"ז עד למות, מחמת המחלוקת על אודות לקיחת הרבנות מאמ"ה, שעל עסק זה היה יואל שוא מנודה שנים רבות, ומוסר מכל כבוד מינוי ופקידות בק"א, כל הימים אשר היה רב"ך חי, ועתה מקרוב איזה שנים קודם בואי לישב באלטונא מת רב"ך, וחזר יואל שוא לכבודו הראשון, ונתמנה פו"מ בק"א, וכן היה בראשית ישיבתי פה. ומיד הרגשתי שלבו אינו שלם, כי כל בני הקהלה באו אלי לקבל פני, אפילו אותן שלא היו אוהבים לאמ"ה ז"ל, וקבלוני בספ"י והבטיחוני לתת כל שאלתי ולהגיד בקשתי ותעש, ולא בקשתי דבר מעמם לכלל ופרט, רק דבר שהותר מכללו: להרשות לי לקבץ מנין בביתי להתפלל בעשרה בתמידות, מאחר שלא יכולתי לילך לבה"כ הגדולה דטריחא לי מילתא טובא, והוא עיקר הסבה שעקרתי מעמדן, ונאותו לי כולם כאמור לעיל, חוץ מהאיש הלז אשר לא בקש לראות פני, ואף ע"פ שעברתי על מדתי, והלכתי אליו לבקרו בביתו, ע"פ עצתו של הרמ"ח ע"ה שהייתי נשמע אליו מתחלה, בהיותו זקן ואני ילד בערכו, ודנתיו ג"כ לזכות, שמא ]מחמת[ היותו זקן וכבד לא בא אלי, כי כבד ממנו הדבר, ועל כן הלכתי לביתו לדרוש שלומו. כסבור הייתי יהא לי ג"כ אוהב נאמן, בפרטות כי לא עלה על דעתי כלל שיהא לי שונא חנם; אבל באמת היה לי לאבן נגף, כי התנגד לי בכח למנוע ולבטל ממני קבוץ עשרה בביתי, אף ע"פ שלא מיחו אפילו לרמ"ח ע"ה שהיה ספרדי ואיש נכרי לקהלה, ואני מבני הרבנים ומילדי הקהל, ולא העמסתי עליהם במאומה. וכל זמן שהיה יואל שוא בקהל, לא הניח לי מעסק זה; כל שבוע היה שולח שמש הקהל אלי, למחות בידי על הדבר הזה, וכל פעם שנסתלק מהחודש שלו היה לי מנוחה מזה, כאשר הגיע חדשו נתחדשה גזרתו, וכ"פ בטלו התמיד בביתי והיה קשה לא לי בלבד, כי גם להאנשים הבאים היה הדבר רע מאד בעיניהם,

willing to set up the wedding canopy until I first paid what [the community [a]] and he [the head of the court R. Y. Ḥ.]
had imposed on me. I will not go on further about his deeds [b].

When I was in Hamburg some weeks before — the matter I already mentioned above — the leader R. Joel Schwab, who had been a
faithful friend of my father, of blessed memory, turned into an enemy of mine because I had taken my lodging in the house
of R. B. K. out of necessity, as said above. These two hated each other to the death, because of the dispute over taking
the rabbinate from my father: over this affair Joel Schwab had been under the ban for many years and excluded from every
honour of appointment and office in the holy community of Altona, all the days that R. B. K. was alive. Now, recently, some
years before I came to live in Altona, R. B. K. died, and Joel Schwab returned to his former honour and was appointed parnas
and leader in the holy community of Altona; and so he was at the beginning of my stay here. At once I felt that his heart
was not whole [with me]. For all the members of the community came to me to welcome me, even those who had not loved my
father, of blessed memory, and received me with a pleasant countenance, and promised to grant all I asked and to fulfil my
request; yet I asked nothing of them at all, except a thing permitted in general: to allow me to gather a quorum in my house
to pray with ten regularly, since I could not go to the Great Synagogue, which was a great burden to me — and this was the
main reason I had left Emden. They all agreed, as said above, except this man, who did not seek to see me. And although I
went against my habit and went to visit him in his house, on the advice of R. M. Ḥ., peace be upon him, whom I obeyed at
first, since he was old and I a child in comparison with him — I judged him favourably too: perhaps [because] he was old
and heavy he had not come to me, for the thing was too heavy for him; therefore I went to his house to ask after his
welfare. I thought he would be a faithful friend to me too, especially as it never entered my mind that he would be my enemy
without cause. But in truth he was "a stone of stumbling" (Isa. 8:14) to me, for he opposed me with force, to prevent and
cancel the gathering of ten in my house — although they had not protested even to R. M. Ḥ., peace be upon him, who was a
Sephardi and a stranger to the community, while I was of the sons of the rabbis and of the children of the community, and
had laid no burden on them at all. And all the time that Joel Schwab was in office in the community he did not let me be in
this matter: every week he sent the community's beadle to me to protest to me about this thing. Each time his month [of
office] ended I had rest from it; when his month came, his decree was renewed, and several times he stopped the regular
prayer in my house. It was hard not for me alone, for to the men who came too the thing was very bad in their eyes,

כי מצאו קורת רוחם להתפלל בלי שמיעת שיחה בטלה כמצויה בבה"כ הגדולה. ופ"א בטלו המנין שלי בימים נוראים וסכות, אז הלכתי אני בבה"כ של הספרדים, והאנשים אשר היו רגילים לבוא אל ביתי לתפלה היו מוכרחים ללכת לבה"כ הגדולה. בתוכם נמצא אדם כשר ירא אלהים ע"ה מאד מגזע גרי צדק; בעי"ט עמד על פתח ביתי, להתאנח על בטול המצוה מביתי, כי לא היתה דעתו נוחה בהליכת בה"כ הגדולה, מטעם שכנים רעים וב"א שאינם הגונים. ומזליה חזי, כי בעו"ה שם נהרג ]הקדוש כ' אפרים[, לפי שראה בעזרת בה"כ אורח קל מסובין, לוקח בפיו שפופרת של טובק במקום הקודש ושואף הענן בפומבי בבית הכנסת, והרע לאיש הטוב וירא שמים הנ"ל, לכן מיחה בקל הדעת, וא"ל שלא יתכן לעשות כן במקום הקודש ובצבור, ולפי שלא אבה האורח לשמוע, הכה כ' אפרים ז"ל שפופרת של האורח והשליכה מפיו; עד"ז גברה החמה של האורח, ונטל סכין ותקעה בבטנו של כ"א ז"ל, ונגע במעיו או בלבו ונתגולל בדמו ובחבלי מיתה כשבעה ימים אחר כך נפטר וחלי"ש [א]. והיה לי צער גדול מאד על אודות האדם כשר הלז, שפגעה בו מדה"ד על אודות יראתו וקנאתו להנ"ל. לזכר עולם יהיה, והמבשלה הזאת תחת מנהיג הקהלה בעו"ה, מידם היתה זאת התקלה, והנ"ל מחל להרוצח על דמו, אכן נשפט בערכאות, המה רצו להיות גואלי הדם, רק מפני שלא רצו עדים להעיד על הרציחה, גם הנרצח כחש, לכן פסקו בדיניהם שישבע הרוצח שלא הכהו נפש ויפטר, וכן עשה ונפטר בדיני אדם. וזה היה הפרי של בטול תפלה מביתי.
עתה אספר מה שעשיתי עוד לטובת חתנו של יואל שוא הנ"ל, וכל זה לא הועיל להסיר המשטמה מלבו, וכך המעשה: שאלוני אז ]הק' נורדשי, סמוך לקביעת ישיבתי בק"א, על אודות ר"ז שטערן חתנו הנ"ל מה טיבו, בשביל ששמעו שיש לו בת וחפץ לשדכה לאחיהם כ' סענדר, ולא רצו לסמוך על שום אדם בענין זה רק עלי, וכאשר אייעץ אותם ככה יעשו; נמצאתי להם והכנסתי א"ע להיות שדכן, מה שלא עשיתי עד עתה. גם כל ימי היותי בעמדן לא נטפלתי בעסק שדוכים, ]כדרך[ רבני אשכנז בכלל, רק אני מנעתי עצמי מזה לשתי סבות, אחת להיותי בלתי בקי כל כך בענייני הקצינים ובניהם ובנותיהם, בלי דרישה

for they found contentment in praying without hearing idle talk, as is common in the Great Synagogue. Once they stopped my
quorum on the Days of Awe and Sukkot. Then I went to the synagogue of the Sephardim, and the men who used to come to my
house for prayer had to go to the Great Synagogue. Among them was a worthy, God-fearing man, very humble, of the stock of
righteous proselytes. On the eve of the festival he stood at the door of my house, sighing over the loss of the
commandment from my house, for he was not easy about going to the Great Synagogue, because of bad neighbours and people who
are not decent. "His star saw it" (b. Megillah 3a): for our many sins, there [the holy R. Ephraim] was killed. For he saw in
the court of the synagogue a light-minded guest who took into his mouth a tobacco pipe in the holy place and drew in the
smoke publicly in the synagogue. This displeased the good and God-fearing man mentioned above, so he protested against the
light-minded man and told him it was not proper to do so in the holy place and in public. Since the guest would not listen,
R. Ephraim, of blessed memory, struck the guest's pipe and threw it from his mouth. At this the guest's wrath grew, and he
took a knife and thrust it into the belly of R. E., of blessed memory, and struck his bowels or his heart; he rolled in his
blood and in the pangs of death about seven days, and afterwards died, "and he shall live and not see the pit" [a]. I
had very great sorrow over this worthy man, on whom the attribute of justice fell because of his fear [of God] and his zeal,
as said above. "Let it be for an everlasting remembrance" (cf. Ex. 17:14): "this ruin was under the hand" (Isa. 3:6) of the
leaders of the community, for our many sins; from them came this stumbling-block. The man mentioned forgave the murderer
his blood; but he was tried in the gentile courts, which wanted to be the avengers of blood. Only, because witnesses would
not testify to the murder, and the murdered man too had denied it, they ruled by their law that the murderer should swear
that he had not struck him mortally, and go free ⟨S: a three-line note, its edge cut off, partly read: "and R. Y. Ḥ. ruled
for him (?) … to swear … falsely"⟩. And so he did, and went free by human law ⟨S: a four-line note: "But in my opinion he
did not rule well; it is written by me in the book She'ilat Ya'avetz(?), part 2 …"⟩. This was the fruit of stopping
the prayer in my house.

Now I will tell what more I did for the good of the son-in-law of Joel Schwab mentioned above; and all this did not help to
remove the enmity from his heart. The story is this. [The leaders] of the Norden family asked me then, near the time I settled in
the holy community of Altona, about R. Z. Stern, his son-in-law mentioned above, what kind of man he was, because they had
heard that he had a daughter, and they wished to match her with their brother R. Sender. They would not rely on anyone in
this matter but me, and as I advised them, so they would do. I was at their service and made myself a matchmaker, which I
had not done until then. All the days I was in Emden I did not engage in matchmaking, [as is the way] of the rabbis of
Ashkenaz in general; I kept myself from it for two reasons: one, because I was not so well acquainted with the affairs of
the leaders and their sons and daughters, without inquiry
